Septuagint base · exhaustive interpretation · not a translation

Ἐν ἀρχῇ
as far as English can be made to carry it

Every load-bearing word is opened to the full range its lexicon gives it, and left open — no single English equivalent is chosen, because choosing one is where the meaning goes. Three parallel readings run against each verse: the apparatus, the unanchored text, and the anchored text. The Old Testament is read from the Greek throughout, so that when the New Testament quotes it, the quotation is visible on the page.

Conventions

Unanchored

The headword is removed entirely. The reader rebuilds the referent from the gloss-chain alone. Best for poetry, prologue, and theological argument, where the familiar word is exactly what stops the reader from seeing.

Anchored

Each word is headed by the first sense its lexicon gives, in the form the text uses, and its chain trails behind, set off by dashes and shaded. Read only the unshaded words for a plain word-for-word rendering; the chains are word for word the unanchored text. Best for narrative, law, and genealogy, where a reader needs to hold a referent across many verses without losing the thread.

Names

Transliterated names keep the form the Greek gives them, with the meaning in parentheses immediately after, in both reading texts. A name left unglossed is a hole in the sentence — it is a word that meant something to the first hearer and means nothing now.

Verbal aspect

Where the Greek aspect carries weight English cannot, it is stated in the text rather than footnoted: one completed act seen whole for the aorist, and kept on being for the imperfect.

The apparatus

Hebrew-to-Greek divergences stay in the notes and never enter the reading text. The Septuagint's own reading is the text; where it parts from the Masoretic Hebrew, that is a fact about the text, not a defect to be quietly repaired.

What is not added

No sense is imported that the Greek word does not carry, however familiar it is from other English versions. Where a well-known English phrase has no basis in this text, the notes say so. Nor are capitals added: the manuscripts have none, so no word is capitalised to make it a title.

Word by word

Under each Greek line, every word with its dictionary form, what its own form adds — tense, voice, mood, case — and the opening senses of its lexicon entry, in the lexicon's order. A concordance stops at the dictionary form; this takes the step after it.

Notes

Lexical range, aspect, and where the Greek parts from the Hebrew

ἐν ἀρχῇ
ἀρχή holds together two things English must split: the temporal origin-point, and ruling precedence. The second sense is alive in ἄρχων, ruler, and in the ἀρχ- of every English word from monarch to architect. Neither sense is optional here.
ἐποίησεν
Aorist active indicative, 3rd singular, of ποιέω — the everyday verb for making and doing, used of potters, poets, and God alike. divergence Hebrew bārā' is a verb that in this stem never takes a human subject. ποιέω takes any subject at all. The exclusivity — this is a thing only God does — is not in the Greek.
ὁ θεός
Articular: the God, the known and definite one. Renders Hebrew Elohim, plural in form but taking singular agreement. Greek has no way to show that and does not try.
τὸν οὐρανόν
divergence Singular. Hebrew šāmayim is a dual or plural form — heavens. The LXX collapses it to one vaulted arch.
τὴν γῆν
γῆ runs from soil underfoot, to farmland, to a country, to dry land as against the sea, to the whole terrestrial realm. Pairing it with οὐρανός pulls toward the widest sense without cancelling the narrow ones.
Capitals
God is capitalised because the lexicon prints it so. The pronouns standing for God in the chain are not: he who is God definitively, the one the article marks out. The manuscripts have no lower case, so a reverential capital is never in the text — it is an editorial decision, and this rendering does not make it.

Notes

Lexical range, aspect, and where the Greek parts from the Hebrew

δέ
A soft adversative, not the hard ἀλλά. It pivots the narrative without contradicting what came before: however, whereas, on the other hand.
ἦν
Imperfect of εἰμί. Durative — a condition that held and kept holding, not a snapshot. English was is aspectually blank, so the duration has to be spelled out.
ἀόρατος καὶ ἀκατασκεύαστος
divergence The single largest departure in the verse, and possibly in the chapter. Hebrew tōhû wā-bōhû is desolation and emptiness — trackless waste, ruin, the wilderness where nothing is. The Greek says invisible and un-outfitted: a thing that exists but is neither perceptible nor yet furnished. On this reading Philo and much of the patristic tradition built a pre-cosmic, formless substrate. It is not what the Hebrew says.
ἀόρατος
Un-seeable, not presenting itself to sight. The same word Paul uses of God himself — the image of the invisible God, Col 1:15.
ἀκατασκεύαστος
Built on κατασκευή: the full outfitting of a house or a ship — fittings, provisions, installed equipment. Formless is too abstract; the word means not yet fitted out.
ἄβυσσος
a-βυσσος, without a sounding — a depth no plumb line reaches. Renders Hebrew tĕhôm, the primeval deep.
πνεῦμα θεοῦ
Anarthrous. πνεῦμα and Hebrew rûaḥ share the same triple range — wind, breath, spirit — one of the rare places where the two languages line up exactly and nothing at all is lost.
ἐπεφέρετο
divergence Imperfect middle-passive of ἐπιφέρω, to be borne upon. Hebrew mĕraḥepet is a bird word — hovering, fluttering, brooding over young, used of an eagle over the nest in Deut 32:11. The Greek is a current, not a wing.
ἐπάνω τοῦ ὕδατος
not in this text The familiar face of the waters is not here. The Hebrew has face of at both points; the LXX drops it at both. ὕδατος is also singular against Hebrew plural mayim.
Capitals
πνεῦμα is printed lowercase in both reading texts. The manuscripts have no lower case at all, so a capital is never in the text: Spirit with a capital would decide for the reader that the word is a title.

Notes

Lexical range, aspect, and where the Greek parts from the Hebrew

συνετελέσθησαν
Aorist passive indicative, 3rd plural, of συντελέω — συν- + τελέω, to bring a thing quite to its end. Passive: the heaven and the earth are not finishing, they are finished. The lexicon's range runs on to make up the whole and make up the number, a sense of completing a count, which is why the chain keeps both.
ὁ κόσμος
Middle Liddell's first sense is order — arrangement, good order, and from there the adornment that gives English cosmetic. The sense world is late and is not the first. divergence Hebrew ṣĕbāʾām is their host, an army: the sun, moon and stars as ranked troops. The Greek keeps the ranking and loses the soldiers.
πᾶς
All, the whole — the whole of a thing taken together, not merely each of its parts. With κόσμος it is the ordered array entire.

Notes

Lexical range, aspect, and where the Greek parts from the Hebrew

τῇ ἡμέρᾳ τῇ ἕκτῃ
The Greek reads on the sixth day where the Hebrew reads on the seventh. divergence The Hebrew has God finishing on the seventh day and resting on it, which reads as though the finishing were itself work done on the sabbath; the Greek removes the difficulty by moving the finishing back a day. The Samaritan Pentateuch and the Syriac agree with the Greek. This is a decision made by translators, and it is visible only if the Greek is read as the text rather than corrected toward the Hebrew.
κατέπαυσεν
Aorist of καταπαύω, whose first sense is transitive — to lay to rest, put an end to, something done to a thing — and whose range runs through make to cease, hinder, check, as far as kill. English rested is intransitive and carries none of that. Hebrew šābat is simply ceased, and gives the sabbath its name.
ἀπὸ πάντων τῶν ἔργων
ἀπό with the genitive: separation, away from. The resting is not inactivity but a standing apart from the works.
ἃ … ὧν
Neuter plural relatives, accusative then genitive: which he made both times, the case changing with the verb that governs it, not the sense. English cannot show the difference.

None in this verse.

Notes

Lexical range, aspect, and where the Greek parts from the Hebrew

ηὐλόγησεν
εὐλογέω, εὖ + λόγος: to speak well of. That is the lexicon's first sense, and to bless is its fourth. The English word bless has drifted so far toward benefaction that the speaking has fallen out of it; the Greek is an act of good speech before it is anything else. Augmented ηὐ- rather than εὐ-, as Rahlfs prints it.
ἡγίασεν
ἁγιάζω has no entry in Middle Liddell at all — it is a word the Septuagint and the New Testament use and the classical language largely does not. LSJ gives it no gloss of its own either: the entry reads = ἁγίζω, and cites this verse. So the sense is ἁγίζω's, hallow, make sacred.
ὅτι
The lexicon prints two entries under this spelling: ὅ τι, for what, wherefore, and the conjunction, that. This is the second. Its range covers both the that of reported speech and the because the sense requires here, and the chain holds them together rather than choosing.
ἤρξατο
Aorist middle of ἄρχω. Perseus opens the entry with in pass. sense:— to be first, a gloss belonging to the passive alone; the first numbered sense, marked "both in Act. and Mid.", is to begin, make a beginning, and that is this form. With the infinitive ποιῆσαι: began to make.
ὧν ἤρξατο ποιῆσαι
divergence Which God began to make. The Hebrew has which God created to make — ʾăšer bārāʾ laʿăśôt, a notoriously hard phrase. The Greek resolves it into a beginning, which the Hebrew does not say.

Notes

Lexical range, aspect, and where the Greek parts from the Hebrew

ἡ βίβλος
Middle Liddell's first sense is the inner bark of the papyrus — the material, before anything is written on it. A book is its third. The headword takes the first sense, which is why this reads as it does: the rule is the lexicon's order, not the expected word, and the seam is left showing.
γενέσεως
γένεσις: an origin, source, productive cause. The book's Greek title, and the word this verse gives it. Genitive, anarthrous. It holds together the origin of a thing and the account of that origin, which English splits into genesis and generations.
ὅτε ἐγένετο
γίνομαι again, against the εἰμί of 1:2 — came to be, not was. Singular, though its subject is heaven and earth together.
Αὕτη … ὅτε
John 1:19, the first verse after the prologue, is built the same way: αὕτη ἐστὶν ἡ μαρτυρία τοῦ Ἰωάννου ὅτε ἀπέστειλαν. A demonstrative, a noun with its genitive, and ὅτε bringing in the occasion; where Genesis has no verb, John supplies ἐστίν. John's prologue has already opened with Genesis's first two words, Ἐν ἀρχῇ. Whether this heading is meant to be heard again the grammar cannot say; that the two are built alike, it can.
ᾗ ἡμέρᾳ
Dative of time without a preposition: on which day. The relative pronoun is the only marker, and English has to supply a preposition the Greek does not print.
τὴν γῆν
The verse ends here with no stop: Rahlfs prints τὴν γῆν and runs straight into καὶ πᾶν χλωρόν in verse 5, one sentence across the verse division. The reading text ends unpunctuated for the same reason.

None in this verse.

Notes

Lexical range, aspect, and where the Greek parts from the Hebrew

χλωρόν
χλωρός is a colour before it is a plant: greenish-yellow, the shade of new growth, of honey, of sand, of a face gone pale. The green thing is named from the colour, not the colour from the thing, and the lexicon's order keeps it that way.
χόρτον
Middle Liddell's first sense is an inclosed place, a feeding-place — the fenced ground, before the fodder standing in it. Grass is its fourth. English has no word that is both the pasture and what grows there, so the headword reads as the enclosure and the chain carries the rest.
πρὸ τοῦ γενέσθαι
πρό with the articular infinitive, twice: before the coming-to-be, before the rising-up. Greek can make a verb into a noun and keep it a verb; English must choose, and loses the action in choosing.
ἔβρεξεν
βρέχω, with ὁ θεός as its subject: God had not rained. Every gloss Perseus tags in the entry's first sense sits inside its :—Pass. clause — to be wetted, get wet — while that sense's own active, to wet (Lat. rigo), it never tags; the second sense, to rain, send rain, it marks as New Testament usage, and that is this form.
οὐκ ἦν ἐργάζεσθαι
εἰμί with the infinitive: there was not a man to work it. The imperfect holds the absence open across the whole stretch of time rather than reporting it once.

None in this verse.

Notes

Lexical range, aspect, and where the Greek parts from the Hebrew

πηγή
Hebrew ʾēd occurs twice in the whole Bible and its sense is not settled — mist, stream, or a flood-word borrowed from Akkadian edû. divergence The Greek does not hedge: πηγή, a spring, water rising from below rather than falling from above. A translator's decision stands where the Hebrew leaves a question.
πηγή, number
Middle Liddell marks its first sense mostly in pl., and prints it running waters, streams; the text has the singular. The headword keeps the lexicon's first translation as the rule requires, and the number is recorded here instead.
ἀνέβαινεν, ἐπότιζεν
Two imperfects: the spring kept going up and kept watering. Against the aorists of verses 1–3, which see an act whole, these hold the action open.
τὸ πρόσωπον τῆς γῆς
Here the Greek does render the Hebrew's face — πρόσωπον for pĕnê hāʾădāmâ — where at both points of 1:2 it dropped it. The difference is the Septuagint's own, and it is why face of the waters must never be written back into that verse while the face of the earth stands correctly in this one.

Notes

Lexical range, aspect, and where the Greek parts from the Hebrew

ἔπλασεν
πλάσσω is the potter's verb, Latin fingere: to work clay or wax into a shape. It gives English plastic and plasma. Not the ἐποίησεν of chapter 1, and not a word used of the heaven and the earth.
χοῦν
The lexicon prints two entries under this spelling: a liquid measure, the Pitcher-feast, and this one — earth thrown down, heaped up, dust. The second is the word here. Double accusative: the man is formed, and dust is what he is formed as.
ἐνεφύσησεν
Middle Liddell gives ἐμφυσάω one gloss, to blow in: to play the flute, where the colon marks a special application of the verb rather than a second sense of it. The verb is blow in; the flute is what blowing in amounts to in Aristophanes. The chain carries both because the lexicon does.
πνοὴν ζωῆς
πνοή's first sense is a blowing — the same first sense the lexicon gives πνεῦμα at 1:2. The two words for moving air stand in the same book with the same opening gloss, and neither is spirit first.
εἰς ψυχὴν ζῶσαν
εἰς of result: the man came to be into something. And ψυχή's first sense in Middle Liddell is breath — so the phrase runs breath into breath: God blows in a blowing, and the man becomes a living breath. English soul arrives only later in the entry and brings a whole anthropology with it that the Greek word does not carry here.
ψυχὴν ζῶσαν
The same phrase the Greek uses of the sea creatures and the beasts in 1:20, 1:24 and again at 2:19. It is not said of the man alone, and a version that renders it living soul here and living creature there has decided something the Greek does not.
Names
None in this verse.

Notes

Lexical range, aspect, and where the Greek parts from the Hebrew

κύριος
The first occurrence in this project. Middle Liddell opens the entry as an adjective, having power; the first noun sense is authority over, lord, and the rule takes the first noun sense. Anarthrous here. It renders the Hebrew divine name, which the Greek does not transliterate but replaces with a title — a substitution made by the translators and invisible in English versions that print LORD.
παράδεισον
A Persian loanword, pairidaēza, a walled enclosure. Middle Liddell's first sense is a park; its second is the garden of Eden, Paradise — the lexicon naming this passage as the source of the English word. Anarthrous: a park, not the.
κατὰ ἀνατολάς
κατά's first sense is down, downwards, and the entry heads all three cases together, so the case cannot be read off it. The idiom κατὰ ἀνατολάς means eastward; ἀνατολή is a rising, and the east is where the rising happens. The reading gives the lexicon's senses and the idiom is recorded here.
ἔθετο
Aorist middle of τίθημι, to set, put, place. The middle carries an interest of the subject's own that English cannot mark.
Εδεμ
name Transliterated, not translated: the Greek keeps the Hebrew ʿĒden, a word for luxury or delight. Whether it is the place-name or the common noun is exactly what the transliteration refuses to decide.

Notes

Lexical range, aspect, and where the Greek parts from the Hebrew

ξύλον
Not δένδρον, the living tree, but ξύλον: wood, cut timber, a piece of wood, a post, a cudgel. The Greek of this chapter names the material rather than the plant, and the same word stands in Acts 5:30 and Galatians 3:13 for the cross.
ἐξανέτειλεν
Middle Liddell gives ἐξανατέλλω a single sense, to spring up from, intransitive, while the LXX uses it here transitively, with God as subject: he made to spring up. With one gloss there is no range to open, so it stands as plain text in both panels and the transitive use is recorded here.
βρῶσιν
βρῶσις opens at meat and goes on to eating and, third, corrosion, rust — the same range Matthew 6:19 uses of what destroys treasure. The tree is good for the eating of it, which is what the chain keeps.
τοῦ εἰδέναι γνωστὸν καλοῦ καὶ πονηροῦ
Word for word: the wood of the to-know knowable of beautiful and of toilsome. divergence The Greek adds γνωστόν, known or knowable, which the Hebrew does not have — ʿēṣ hadda'at ṭôb wārāʿ is simply the tree of the knowledge of good and evil. And πονηρός's first sense is toilsome, painful, grievous: the word for evil begins as the word for hard labour.
ἐν μέσῳ τῷ παραδείσῳ
Dative, not the genitive ἐν μέσῳ τοῦ παραδείσου that classical Greek would want. The construction is a Hebraism; Rahlfs prints it as it stands.

Notes

Lexical range, aspect, and where the Greek parts from the Hebrew

ἐκπορεύεται, ἀφορίζεται
Both present, in the middle of a past narrative: the river goes out and is divided, not went and was. The tense makes the geography contemporary with whoever is reading.
ἐκπορεύομαι
Middle Liddell files the deponent under its active, ἐκπορεύω, whose first gloss is to make to go out, fetch out — the active alone. The middle glosses it tags next, to go out and forth, march out, are this form, and the headword takes the first of those.
ἀρχάς
The word that opened Genesis and John: ἀρχή, a beginning, and also rule, headship. Here it is the head of a river — where a stream begins. The same noun, and the reading keeps the whole range so the connection stays visible.
Εδεμ
Second occurrence in the chapter, so it stands bare: glossed once at 2:8.

Lexical range, aspect, and where the Greek parts from the Hebrew

ὄνομα τῷ ἑνί
A name to the one — no copula, as Hebrew does it. The reading supplies nothing, because nothing is there to supply.
ὁ κυκλῶν
Articular present participle of κυκλόω, to encircle, surround: the one that goes round. Present, and so still going round.
χρυσίον
The diminutive of χρυσός: Middle Liddell's first sense is a piece of gold, then gold as a substance, then coined money. The Greek names a nugget before it names the metal.
Φισων, Ευιλατ
name Both transliterated with no attempt at sense. Ευιλατ is Hebrew Ḥăwîlâ, usually connected with ḥôl, sand; Φισων is Pîšôn, of uncertain derivation, perhaps from pûš, to leap or spring. Neither river has been identified.

Notes

Lexical range, aspect, and where the Greek parts from the Hebrew

ἄνθραξ
Middle Liddell gives one sense: charcoal, coal. The gem is named from the burning coal it looks like, which is how Latin carbunculus, a little coal, became the carbuncle. The Greek word says coal and the context says stone; the reading prints the word.
ὁ λίθος ὁ πράσινος
Middle Liddell has no πράσινος at all. LSJ gives leek-green, light green, from πράσον, a leek — and cites this very verse for the stone: λίθος π. = πρασῖτις. Its later sense, the green faction, belongs to the chariot-racing of the Circus and is not in play.
καλόν
No copula again: the gold of that land, beautiful. And καλός is beautiful before it is good — the judgement on the gold is aesthetic first.

Αἰθιοπίας

Γηων
name Hebrew Gîḥôn, from gîaḥ, to burst or gush forth — a name for a spring that breaks out of the ground. Jerusalem's own spring carries the same name in 1 Kings 1:33.

Notes

Lexical range, aspect, and where the Greek parts from the Hebrew

ὁ πορευόμενος
Middle Liddell files πορεύομαι under the active πορεύω, whose sense I is marked Act. — to make to go, carry, convey — and cannot be this form. Sense II is marked Pass. and Mid., and its first gloss is to be driven or carried, with to go, walk, march following. The middle is available to both, so nothing is skipped inside it and the headword takes its first translation. A river that is carried along is not a strained reading of a current.
κατέναντι
The entry in Middle Liddell carries no translation at all: it reads κατέναντι = κατεναντίον, and the senses are the ones that entry gives — over against, opposite, before. A cross-reference followed, not a sense chosen.
Τίγρις, Εὐφράτης
name Both are Greek forms of Old Persian names rather than of the Hebrew. The Hebrew has Ḥiddeqel and Pĕrāt; the Greek prints Τίγρις, from tigrā, an arrow, for the speed of the current, and Εὐφράτης, from Ufrātu. Two rivers that exist, after two that no one has found.
Ἀσσυρίων
name The Assyrians, named from Aššur — their god, their first city, and their land at once. Genitive plural: the river runs opposite them, not opposite the country.

Notes

Lexical range, aspect, and where the Greek parts from the Hebrew

ἐργάζεσθαι αὐτὸν καὶ φυλάσσειν
αὐτόν is masculine and refers to παράδεισος, not to the man: he is to work it. English it hides the agreement; the Greek cannot be misread.
φυλάσσειν
φυλάσσω opens at to keep watch and ward, keep guard — a sentry's word, used of garrisons and of watching by night. What the garden needs is not only cultivation but a guard, and the verb says so before it says keep.
Αδαμ
Still ὁ ἄνθρωπος here, the man. The name does not arrive until the next verse, and the Greek keeps the common noun until then.

Notes

Lexical range, aspect, and where the Greek parts from the Hebrew

τῷ Αδαμ
name The name enters, and the Greek prints it bare — Αδαμ, indeclinable, with the article carrying the case. Hebrew ʾādām is the common noun man, from ʾădāmâ, the ground he was formed from; Greek keeps the sound and loses the pun, which is why the gloss carries it.
βρώσει φάγῃ
A dative noun before its own verb: with eating you shall eat. It renders the Hebrew infinitive absolute, which intensifies — you may freely eat — by a construction Greek does not have and so imitates word for word. The reading keeps the imitation rather than smoothing it to an adverb.
Ἀπὸ
Capitalised because it opens direct speech, as Rahlfs prints it; listed in this verse's `speech` field so the checks do not take it for a proper name.

Notes

Lexical range, aspect, and where the Greek parts from the Hebrew

τοῦ γινώσκειν
A different verb from 2:9. There the tree is τοῦ εἰδέναι, from οἶδα — to know, the knowledge one simply has. Here it is τοῦ γινώσκειν, from γινώσκω — to learn to know, to perceive, to mark, knowledge that is come by. The same tree, named twice, with two words English renders alike.
φάγεσθε, φάγητε, ἀποθανεῖσθε
All plural, where 2:16 had the singular φάγῃ. The permission is addressed to the man alone; the prohibition is already addressed to more than one, several verses before the woman is made.
θανάτῳ ἀποθανεῖσθε
The same construction as βρώσει φάγῃ, and the same Hebrew idiom behind it: with death you shall die. Not you shall surely die — that is the idiom resolved; the Greek leaves it standing.
ἀπʼ
Elided before a vowel, three times. The mark is printed in Rahlfs and written here as U+02BC, the character the SBLGNT uses, so one convention covers both testaments.

Notes

Lexical range, aspect, and where the Greek parts from the Hebrew

Οὐ καλὸν
καλός is beautiful before it is good, so what is denied here is in the first place a fitness, a rightness of form. Against the refrain of chapter 1 — καὶ εἶδεν ὁ θεὸς ὅτι καλόν — this is the single negation.
ποιήσωμεν
First person plural subjunctive: let us make, as at 1:26. The Greek reproduces the Hebrew plural exactly and adds nothing to explain it.
βοηθὸν κατʼ αὐτόν
βοηθός is an entry that opens as an adjective, assisting, auxiliary; the first noun sense is an assistant. The word is used in the Septuagint of God himself as the helper of Israel, so it carries no implication of lesser rank. κατά with the accusative — the same preposition as κατὰ ἀνατολάς — renders Hebrew kĕnegdô, corresponding to him.

Notes

Lexical range, aspect, and where the Greek parts from the Hebrew

ἰδεῖν
Aorist infinitive of ὁράω: God brings the animals to see what the man would call them. The subject of the seeing is left open — it can be God's seeing or the man's — and Greek does not resolve it.
ψυχὴν ζῶσαν
The same phrase used of the man at 2:7, here of every animal. The Greek makes no distinction of kind between them at this point, and a version that renders it living soul of the man and living creature of the beasts has made one.
ἔπλασεν … ἔτι
divergence And God formed yet — the animals are formed after the man, as chapter 2 has it, where chapter 1 has them before. The Greek ἔτι, still, further, marks the continuation plainly rather than smoothing the order; some English versions render a pluperfect, had formed, which the Greek does not say.
Αδαμ
Twice here, both bare: glossed once at 2:16.

Notes

Lexical range, aspect, and where the Greek parts from the Hebrew

κτήνεσιν
κτῆνος opens at flocks and herds — property, from κτάομαι, to acquire. The domestic animals are named by their belonging to someone, where θηρία are named by their wildness.
οὐχ εὑρέθη
Aorist passive: was not found. Not there was none — the Greek reports a search that came to nothing, which is what makes the verse the hinge of the chapter.
ὅμοιος αὐτῷ
Like to him, where 2:18 had κατʼ αὐτόν, corresponding to him. The Greek uses two different phrases for the one Hebrew kĕnegdô, and the reading keeps both rather than levelling them.
— the dash
Rahlfs prints a dash after αὐτῷ, marking the break before the sleep falls. It is the editor's paragraph mark rather than a word of the text, so it stands in the Greek line and not in the reading.

Notes

Lexical range, aspect, and where the Greek parts from the Hebrew

ἔκστασιν
Not sleep but ἔκστασις — a standing outside oneself. Middle Liddell gives it as any displacement: entrancement, astonishment, and then a trance. It is the word used of Peter on the roof in Acts 10:10 and of the women at the tomb in Mark 16:8. The Hebrew tardēmâ is a deep sleep; the Greek makes it a displacement of the mind.
ὕπνωσεν
The lexicon's first sense is transitive and causative, to put to sleep; to fall asleep, sleep is its second. The Septuagint uses the active intransitively here — he slept — and the headword keeps the lexicon's order with the note carrying the usage.
μίαν τῶν πλευρῶν
πλευρά is a rib, and also the side — of a body, an army, a building, a page. Greek does not choose, and neither does the reading. One of his ribs and one of his sides are the same phrase.
ἀνεπλήρωσεν σάρκα
ἀναπληρόω is to fill up, to make good a deficiency — used of filling a gap in a line of troops or paying a debt in full. The flesh does not replace the rib so much as make the place whole again.

Notes

Lexical range, aspect, and where the Greek parts from the Hebrew

ᾠκοδόμησεν
οἰκοδομέω is built from οἶκος and δέμω: to build a house, which Middle Liddell gives as its first sense before the general to build. The rib is built into a woman with the verb used of masonry, and the Hebrew bānâ does the same.
εἰς γυναῖκα
εἰς of result again, as at 2:7 where the man came to be εἰς ψυχὴν ζῶσαν. The rib is built into a woman: the preposition marks what it became.
πρὸς τὸν Αδαμ
πρός with the accusative, the directional preposition of John 1:1 — toward, facing, in address toward. She is not delivered to him but brought facing him.

Notes

Lexical range, aspect, and where the Greek parts from the Hebrew

γυνή … ἀνδρός
The Hebrew turns on a pun: ʾiššâ, woman, from ʾîš, man. divergence Greek γυνή and ἀνήρ are unrelated words, and the reason clause — she shall be called woman, because she was taken out of her man — loses the thing that made it a reason. The Greek keeps the sentence and drops its hinge; no English version can recover it either, because English woman and man only look related.
ἀνδρός
ἀνήρ, not ἄνθρωπος: the male, against the human being of 2:7 and 2:15. This is the first time the chapter distinguishes them, and both would be man in English, which is why the notes must say which is which.
ὀστοῦν
The Attic contraction of ὀστέον. Middle Liddell has the entry but tags no usable translation in it — only the, sliced out of a quoted phrase — so the sense here is LSJ's, bone.
Τοῦτο
Neuter — this thing, not this woman — and capitalised because it opens direct speech; listed in `speech` so the checks do not take it for a name.

Notes

Lexical range, aspect, and where the Greek parts from the Hebrew

οἱ δύο
The two is not in the Hebrew, which reads only and they shall become one flesh. divergence The Greek supplies the number, and every New Testament quotation of the verse — Matthew 19:5, Mark 10:8, 1 Corinthians 6:16, Ephesians 5:31 — quotes the Greek with it. A phrase added by translators became the text the apostles argued from, which is the whole case for reading the Old Testament in Greek.
προσκολληθήσεται
προσκολλάω is to glue on: κόλλα is glue, and English collagen and protocol are its relatives. Future passive in form — he will be glued — where English makes it active, shall cleave.
ἄνθρωπος
Anarthrous and general: a human being, not the man of the story. The verse steps out of the narrative into a rule.

Notes

Lexical range, aspect, and where the Greek parts from the Hebrew

ᾐσχύνοντο
Imperfect, middle or passive — the two share one form in this tense. αἰσχύνω's active senses are to make ugly, disfigure, mar and to dishonour; the first numbered sense open to this voice is to be ashamed, feel shame, and that is the one taken. The imperfect holds it open: they were not, and kept on not being, ashamed.
γυμνοί
γυμνός runs from naked through unarmed to uncovered — the word behind gymnasium, where the exercise was done stripped. It is not only a state of dress but of defencelessness, and the next chapter turns on that.
ὅ τε Αδαμ
τε couples closely: both Adam and his wife, taken as one pair rather than two parties. Rahlfs prints the article ὅ before the indeclinable name.

Middle/passive marks a tense in which the two voices share one form; masculine/feminine, an adjective whose form does not distinguish them.

Notes

Lexical range, aspect, and where the Greek parts from the Hebrew

ὄφις
Middle Liddell gives one sense, a serpent, snake. The noun carries no judgement of its own; what the serpent is, the verse says with an adjective.
φρονιμώτατος
Superlative of φρόνιμος, whose first sense is in one's right mind, in one's senses; staid, discreet is its second and wise, sensible, prudent its third. It is not a word for cunning, and it is the adjective of Matthew 10:16: γίνεσθε οὖν φρόνιμοι ὡς οἱ ὄφεις. divergence Hebrew ʿārûm, shrewd, crafty, puns on ʿărûmmîm, naked, in 2:25. Greek γυμνοί and φρόνιμος share nothing, and the pun is gone.
τῶν θηρίων τῶν ἐπὶ τῆς γῆς
The wild animals upon the earth. divergence The Hebrew has ḥayyat haśśādeh, the living things of the field. The Greek widens the field to the earth, and does so again at 3:14.
κύριος ὁ θεός
The chapter's first κύριος: the title the Greek sets in place of the Hebrew divine name, as at 2:8.
Τί ὅτι
τί in the accusative with ὅτι, why is it that — the construction of Luke 2:49, Τί ὅτι ἐζητεῖτέ με. divergence The Hebrew ʾap kî-ʾāmar ʾĕlōhîm is an exclamation as much as a question, Indeed, has God said…; the Greek asks for God's reason.
Οὐ μὴ φάγητε
οὐ μή with the aorist subjunctive, the strongest denial Greek has: by no means may you eat. At 2:16 every tree but one was given; the serpent's version forbids them all, and the construction makes the overstatement emphatic.
Τί, Οὐ
Capitalised because each opens direct speech — the serpent's question, and the words it puts in God's mouth, as Rahlfs prints it; listed in `speech` so the checks do not take them for a proper name.

φαγόμεθα

καρποῦ

Notes

Lexical range, aspect, and where the Greek parts from the Hebrew

οὐδὲ μὴ ἅψησθε αὐτοῦ
Nor may you touch it. The command as 2:16–17 gives it, in Greek and in Hebrew alike, says nothing of touching. The woman's report adds it.
ἅψησθε
Middle of ἅπτω. The entry's first sense, to fasten, bind fast, is the active; its second is marked Mid. and takes the genitive, as here — to fasten oneself to, cling to, hang on by, lay hold of, grasp, touch. The headword takes that sense, the form's own.
ἀπʼ αὐτοῦ … αὐτοῦ
Masculine. The pronoun takes up the fronted ἀπὸ καρποῦ, repeating its preposition, not the neuter ξύλον beside it: it is the fruit that may not be eaten or touched.
ὅ ἐστιν ἐν μέσῳ τοῦ παραδείσου
At 2:9 it was the tree of life that stood ἐν μέσῳ; the woman places the forbidden tree there. Revelation 2:7 describes the tree of life with nearly the same clause: ἐκ τοῦ ξύλου τῆς ζωῆς, ὅ ἐστιν ἐν τῷ παραδείσῳ τοῦ θεοῦ.
ἵνα
An adverb of place in the lexicon's first sense, there, where, and a conjunction in its second, that, in order that. Used as a conjunction, it takes the first conjunction sense, as a word used as a noun takes the first noun sense.
Οὐ
Capitalised because it opens direct speech — the command as the woman repeats it, as Rahlfs prints it; listed in `speech` so the checks do not take it for a proper name.

Notes

Lexical range, aspect, and where the Greek parts from the Hebrew

ᾔδει
Pluperfect of οἶδα, whose perfect is a present, I know; its pluperfect is a past, knew. divergence The Hebrew yōdēaʿ is a participle, God knows. The Greek puts the knowing in the past.
ἐν ᾗ ἂν ἡμέρᾳ φάγητε ἀπʼ αὐτοῦ
God's words from 2:17, ᾗ δʼ ἂν ἡμέρᾳ φάγητε ἀπʼ αὐτοῦ, taken up with ἐν added — and given another ending.
ὡς θεοί
Plural: as gods. divergence Hebrew kēʾlōhîm can be read like God or like gods, since ʾĕlōhîm is plural in form either way. The Greek must decide, and decides for the plural.
ὡς
One Middle Liddell entry holds two words: ὥς, accented, the demonstrative so, thus, and ὡς, the relative as. Rahlfs prints the relative, and its glosses are the chain.
γινώσκοντες
γινώσκω, not οἶδα: the verb of the tree's name at 2:17, knowledge come by. Present participle — knowing as a lasting condition.

Notes

Lexical range, aspect, and where the Greek parts from the Hebrew

ἀρεστὸν … ὡραῖον … κατανοῆσαι
Three things seen: beautiful for eating, acceptable to the eyes to look at, and produced at the right season to observe. κατανοέω is to observe well, to understand — to take something in with the mind. divergence The Hebrew has a delight to the eyes and desirable to make one wise, lĕhaśkîl. The Greek keeps the looking and loses the wanting: nothing in the sentence desires wisdom.
ἔφαγον
Third plural, they ate. divergence The Hebrew wayyōʾkal is singular, and he ate. The Greek has the man and the woman eat together.
καὶ τῷ ἀνδρί
καί here is also: she gave also to her man. ἀνήρ, the male, as at 2:23 — not ἄνθρωπος.
μετʼ αὐτῆς
μετά with the genitive opens at in the midst of, among; along with is its second sense and with its third. The Hebrew has the same, ʿimmāh, with her.

Notes

Lexical range, aspect, and where the Greek parts from the Hebrew

διηνοίχθησαν
The serpent's verb from 3:5, διανοιχθήσονται, now in the aorist: the promise is kept in the words it was made in. διανοίγω is to open; its second sense, to open and explain, is the New Testament's — Luke 24:32, ὡς διήνοιγεν ἡμῖν τὰς γραφάς.
ἔγνωσαν
γινώσκω, the verb of the tree at 2:17 and of the promise at 3:5. What they come to know is that they are naked.
γυμνοὶ ἦσαν
The word of 2:25, where it stood beside not ashamed, and the same imperfect, ἦσαν. γυμνός runs on to unarmed, uncovered.
περιζώματα
A girdle round the loins, apron — a band, not a garment. Hebrew ḥăgōrōt, belts, is the same.

Notes

Lexical range, aspect, and where the Greek parts from the Hebrew

τὸ δειλινόν
Accusative of time, at evening. Middle Liddell files δειλινός as a contraction of δειελινός and gives that entry one sense, at evening, so there is no range to open and it stands as plain text. divergence The Hebrew is lĕrûaḥ hayyôm, at the wind of the day — rûaḥ, the word behind πνεῦμα at 1:2. The Greek gives the hour and drops the wind.
τὴν φωνὴν … περιπατοῦντος
φωνή's first sense is a sound, tone; the voice follows it. The participle is genitive masculine, so it goes with κυρίου τοῦ θεοῦ, not with φωνήν: the sound of the lord God, walking. Hebrew qôl is likewise both sound and voice.
ἐκρύβησαν
Aorist passive of κρύπτω, were hidden. The entry gives the passive its own gloss, to hide oneself, lie hidden, and the chain carries both.
ἀπὸ προσώπου
From face — πρόσωπον again, and here the Greek keeps the Hebrew's face, mippĕnê, as it did at 2:6.
Αδαμ
name First occurrence in this chapter, so glossed again.

Notes

Lexical range, aspect, and where the Greek parts from the Hebrew

ἐφοβήθην
Aorist passive of φοβέομαι, which Middle Liddell files under φοβέω. The entry's actives — to put to flight, to terrify — are skipped by name; its passive opens to be put to flight, to flee affrighted, and only after that to be seized with fear, fear. In the lexicon's order, fear is a running away before it is a feeling.
περιπατοῦντος
Genitive, with σου: your sound, walking. divergence The Hebrew has I heard the sound of you in the garden; the Greek adds walking, from 3:8.
ὅτι γυμνός εἰμι
Present: I am naked. The next verse asks how he knows it.
Τὴν
Capitalised because it opens direct speech, as Rahlfs prints it; listed in `speech` so the checks do not take it for a proper name.

Notes

Lexical range, aspect, and where the Greek parts from the Hebrew

εἶ; μή
Rahlfs's punctuation, which his apparatus marks as his: a question, then a second one opened by μή, which expects no — you did not eat from the tree…, did you? variant Codex Alexandrinus reads εἶ, εἰ μή: who told you that you are naked, unless you ate from the tree… — one question, with its answer inside it.
τούτου μόνου
Of this one alone. divergence Not in the Hebrew, which has which I commanded you not to eat from. The Greek narrows the command to the single tree, in God's own words, and does so again at 3:17.
ἀνήγγειλεν
ἀναγγέλλω, to carry back tidings of, report — news brought back from somewhere.
Τίς
Capitalised because it opens direct speech, as Rahlfs prints it; listed in `speech` so the checks do not take it for a proper name.

Notes

Lexical range, aspect, and where the Greek parts from the Hebrew

ἠπάτησεν
ἀπατάω, to cheat, trick, outwit, beguile. 2 Corinthians 11:3 uses the compound of this moment, ὡς ὁ ὄφις ἐξηπάτησεν Εὕαν, and 1 Timothy 2:14 has both verbs: Ἀδὰμ οὐκ ἠπατήθη, ἡ δὲ γυνὴ ἐξαπατηθεῖσα.
Τί τοῦτο ἐποίησας;
τί as at 3:1, why, with τοῦτο the object: why did you do this? The Hebrew mah-zōʾt ʿāśît is what is this you have done?
Τί, Ὁ
Capitalised because each opens direct speech — God's question, and the woman's answer, as Rahlfs prints it; listed in `speech` so the checks do not take them for a proper name.

Notes

Lexical range, aspect, and where the Greek parts from the Hebrew

ἐπικατάρατος
Middle Liddell gives one sense, yet more accursed — ἐπί added to κατάρατος, accursed — so there is no range to open and it stands as plain text. ἀπὸ πάντων is comparative, after the Hebrew min: accursed beyond all the flocks and the wild animals. Galatians 3:13 quotes the word from Deuteronomy: Ἐπικατάρατος πᾶς ὁ κρεμάμενος ἐπὶ ξύλου.
τῶν θηρίων τῆς γῆς
divergence Of the earth, where the Hebrew has of the field, as at 3:1.
ἐπὶ τῷ στήθει σου καὶ τῇ κοιλίᾳ
κοιλία's first sense is the large cavity of the body; the belly follows. divergence The Hebrew has only ʿal-gĕḥōnĕkā, upon your belly. The Greek adds the breast.
γῆν φάγῃ
You will eat earth. divergence Hebrew ʿāpār, dust, which the Greek rendered χοῦν at 2:7 and renders γῆ here and at 3:19.
πορεύσῃ
Future of πορεύομαι, the verb of the Tigris at 2:14: being driven, carried, going.
Ὅτι
Capitalised because it opens direct speech, as Rahlfs prints it; listed in `speech` so the checks do not take it for a proper name.

Senses: Middle Liddell (1889; Perseus Digital Library, CC BY-SA 3.0 US), in the lexicon's own order, without regard to context; LSJ (PerseusDL, CC BY-SA 4.0) where Middle Liddell has no entry. Middle/passive marks a tense in which the two voices share one form; masculine/feminine, an adjective whose form does not distinguish them.

Notes

Lexical range, aspect, and where the Greek parts from the Hebrew

αὐτός
Masculine, where σπέρμα before it is neuter; a pronoun agreeing with it would be αὐτό. The Hebrew hûʾ is masculine and agrees with zeraʿ, which is masculine in Hebrew. Read as agreeing by sense with a collective seed, the Greek means the offspring; read as a single male descendant, it means one person. The grammar permits both and does not choose between them.
τηρήσει … τηρήσεις
τηρέω, to watch over, protect, guard, then to watch narrowly, to watch for — the same verb both times. divergence The Hebrew uses šûp twice, a verb whose sense is disputed: bruise, crush, or snap at. The Greek has a verb of watching, not of striking.
ἀνὰ μέσον
ἀνά with the accusative, up to, up along, with μέσον, the middle: together the idiom between. The reading gives the lexicon's parts and the idiom is recorded here, as κατὰ ἀνατολάς was at 2:8.
σπέρματος
σπέρμα's first sense is that which is sown — the seed of plants — then offspring, issue, then race, descent.
ἔχθραν
Middle Liddell heads the entry with the Ionic spelling, ἔχθρη: hatred, enmity, hostility.

Notes

Lexical range, aspect, and where the Greek parts from the Hebrew

ἡ ἀποστροφή σου
ἀποστροφή is a turning back, then a turning away from, an escape, then a resort, resource. No verb: toward your man, your turning. divergence The Hebrew is tĕšûqātēk, your desire. The Greek word is the one that renders tĕšûbātēk, your return — a word one letter away.
τὸν στεναγμόν σου
Your sighing, groaning, moaning. divergence The Hebrew is hērōnēk, your conception, your pregnancy.
Πληθύνων πληθυνῶ
Participle and finite verb of one root, multiplying I will multiply: Greek imitating the Hebrew infinitive absolute, harbâ ʾarbeh, as βρώσει φάγῃ did at 2:16.
τέξῃ τέκνα
Verb and object from one root, τίκτω and τέκνον. The lexicon's first sense for τέκνον is that which is borne; a child comes with it.
Πληθύνων
Capitalised because it opens direct speech, as Rahlfs prints it; listed in `speech` so the checks do not take it for a proper name.

Notes

Lexical range, aspect, and where the Greek parts from the Hebrew

τριβόλους
τρίβολος is first a caltrop, a three-spiked iron thrown down to lame an enemy's horses; a prickly plant, a burr, thistle is its second sense, marked New Testament. Hebrews 6:8 has the pair from this verse: ἐκφέρουσα δὲ ἀκάνθας καὶ τριβόλους.
ἀνατελεῖ
ἀνατέλλω, the verb of 2:5, where nothing had yet risen up from the ground.
τὸν χόρτον τοῦ ἀγροῦ
χόρτος and ἀγρός as at 2:5, where there was not yet any χόρτος ἀγροῦ. Now the man is to eat it.

Notes

Lexical range, aspect, and where the Greek parts from the Hebrew

γῆ εἶ καὶ εἰς γῆν ἀπελεύσῃ
divergence The Hebrew is ʿāpār ʾattâ wĕʾel-ʿāpār tāšûb, dust you are and to dust you will return. The Greek has γῆ, earth, both times — not the χοῦς of 2:7 — and for return it has ἀπέρχομαι, to go away, depart. The verb of returning, ἀποστρέφω, stands earlier in the verse, for the Hebrew's first šûb.
ἕως τοῦ ἀποστρέψαι σε
ἕως with the articular infinitive, a construction Middle Liddell cites in the entry itself, ἕως τοῦ ἀποτῖσαι. ἀποστρέφω's first sense is transitive, to turn; here σε is its subject, and the use is the entry's intransitive, to turn back.
ἐξ ἧς ἐλήμφθης
Out of which you were taken — the verb of the rib at 2:22–23, now of the man and the earth.
— the dash
Rahlfs's paragraph dash, as after 2:20. It stands in the Greek line and not in the reading.

Ζωή … τῶν ζώντων
Translating the name keeps the verse's reason intact: Ζωή, because she is mother of all τῶν ζώντων. divergence At 4:1 the Greek transliterates the same name, Ευαν, and the play is not made again.
μήτηρ πάντων
No verb: this one, mother of all the living. The Hebrew has hāyĕtâ, she was.

Notes

Lexical range, aspect, and where the Greek parts from the Hebrew

χιτῶνας δερματίνους
χιτών is the garment worn next the skin, a frock — the tunic, with a mantle over it — and δερμάτινος is of skin, leathern. The περιζώματα of 3:7 were girdles; these are garments.
ἐνέδυσεν
ἐνδύω's first sense, to go into, put on, is dressing oneself; the entry marks the aorist ἐνέδυσα causal, to clothe another, and that is this form. They are clothed; they do not dress.
— the dash
Rahlfs's paragraph dash again, in the Greek line and not in the reading.

Notes

Lexical range, aspect, and where the Greek parts from the Hebrew

ὁ θεός
Rahlfs prints ὁ θεός alone, with Codex Coislinianus (M). variant Codex Alexandrinus reads κύριος ὁ θεός, and Origen's recension carries κύριος under the asterisk — his sign for words in the Hebrew that the Greek lacked. The Hebrew has YHWH ʾĕlōhîm.
Αδαμ
divergence Hebrew hāʾādām, with the article: the man. The Greek reads the name.
γέγονεν
Perfect of γίνομαι: not became but has come to be, and stands so.
ὡς εἷς ἐξ ἡμῶν
First person plural in God's mouth, as ποιήσωμεν at 2:18. The Greek renders it exactly and adds nothing to explain it.
μήποτε … ζήσεται
Three subjunctives under μήποτε — lest he stretch out, take, eat — and then a future indicative, ζήσεται, and he will live: the last verb states an outcome, not a fear. Neither the Greek nor the Hebrew finishes the sentence; what God does follows in 3:23.
εἰς τὸν αἰῶνα
αἰών is first a period of existence, one's life-time, then an age, then a long space of time; the lexicon records εἰς τοὺς αἰῶνας as for ever. The idiom is noted here and the reading prints the lexicon's range.
Ἰδοὺ
Capitalised because it opens direct speech, as Rahlfs prints it; listed in `speech` so the checks do not take it for a proper name.

Notes

Lexical range, aspect, and where the Greek parts from the Hebrew

τοῦ παραδείσου τῆς τρυφῆς
The park of softness, of luxury. divergence The Hebrew is gan-ʿēden, the garden of Eden. At 2:8 and 2:10 the Greek transliterated the name, Εδεμ; here it translates it with τρυφή — softness, delicacy, luxury — the sense ʿēden has as a common noun.
ἐξαπέστειλεν
ἐξαποστέλλω, a double compound, ἐκ and ἀπό with στέλλω: to send quite away.
ἐργάζεσθαι τὴν γῆν
The task of 2:5, where there was no man to work the earth, and of 2:15, where he was set in the park to work it. The same verb, now outside.

Notes

Lexical range, aspect, and where the Greek parts from the Hebrew

κατῴκισεν αὐτὸν ἀπέναντι
divergence The Hebrew has wayyaškēn miqqedem lĕgan-ʿēden ʾet-hakkĕrubîm, and he stationed east of the garden of Eden the cherubim. The Greek makes the man the object — he settled him opposite the park — and gives the cherubim a verb of their own, ἔταξεν.
κατῴκισεν
κατοικίζω, to remove to a place, and settle or establish there as colonists: the verb of founding a colony.
τὰ χερουβιμ
name Transliterated, and neuter here, τά. Rahlfs prints the Hebrew plural ending in -ιμ; Codex Alexandrinus has -ιν, as Hebrews 9:5 does, Χερουβὶν δόξης. τάσσω is to arrange, put in order, first of troops drawn up for battle.
τὴν φλογίνην ῥομφαίαν τὴν στρεφομένην
Middle Liddell has no φλόγινος; LSJ gives flaming, fiery and cites this verse. ῥομφαία is a large sword, scymitar, a Thracian blade — the word of Luke 2:35 and of the sword from the mouth in Revelation 1:16. The participle is middle or passive, and the entry's passive and middle open to turn oneself, to turn round.
φυλάσσειν τὴν ὁδόν
φυλάσσω, to keep watch and ward, the verb of 2:15, where the man was set in the park to guard it. The lexicon prints two entries under ὁδός; the first is the Attic word for a threshold, and the way is the second.

Notes

Lexical range, aspect, and where the Greek parts from the Hebrew

ἔγνω
γινώσκω, to learn to know, perceive: the verb the Hebrew yādaʿ uses of a man's union with his wife, and the Greek keeps it — the verb of knowing good and evil at 2:17 and 3:5.
συλλαβοῦσα
συλλαμβάνω's first sense is to collect, gather together; to conceive, of women, is its fourth. The headword keeps the lexicon's order, and the chain ends where the verse means.
Ἐκτησάμην … Καιν
κτάομαι, to procure for oneself, to get, gain, acquire. divergence The Hebrew names Qayin from qānîtî, I have gotten. The Greek keeps the sense and loses the sound, so the name no longer explains itself.
διὰ τοῦ θεοῦ
Through God. divergence The Hebrew is ʾet-YHWH, with YHWH, and uses the divine name; the Greek has θεός, with a preposition of agency.
Ευαν
name Here the Greek transliterates the name it translated at 3:20: Hebrew Ḥawwâ, which was Ζωή there, is Ευα here, Ευαν in the accusative. The play on life is not made again.
Αδαμ, Καιν
name Αδαμ is glossed again, first in this chapter. Καιν is Hebrew Qayin.
Ἐκτησάμην
Capitalised because it opens direct speech, as Rahlfs prints it; listed in `speech` so the checks do not take it for a proper name.

Notes

Lexical range, aspect, and where the Greek parts from the Hebrew

προσέθηκεν τεκεῖν
Put to bearing: προστίθημι with an infinitive, a Hebraism for doing a thing again, wattōsep lāledet. The lexicon's first sense is to put to; to add is its third.
ποιμὴν προβάτων
Middle Liddell has no ποιμήν — only the Doric ποιμάν, a cross-reference to the entry the abridgement lacks — so the sense is LSJ's: herdsman, then shepherd, citing this verse. πρόβατον is, in the lexicon's own word, properly anything that walks forward: cattle and flocks in Homer, horses in Herodotus, and in Attic always sheep.
Αβελ
name Hebrew Hebel, breath, vapour, a word used elsewhere for what is empty. The transliteration keeps only the sound.
ἦν ἐργαζόμενος
Imperfect with a participle: was working — Cain's occupation as a continuing state, beside ἐγένετο for Abel's.

Notes

θυσίαν
θυσία is an offering, then sacrifices, sacred rites, then the victim. divergence The Hebrew calls both offerings minḥâ, a gift. The Greek gives Cain's θυσία, here and at 4:5, and Abel's δῶρα at 4:4 — two words where the Hebrew has one.
μεθʼ ἡμέρας

ἤνεγκεν

Notes

ἐπὶ τοῖς δώροις αὐτοῦ
Hebrews 11:4 takes the phrase word for word — μαρτυροῦντος ἐπὶ τοῖς δώροις αὐτοῦ τοῦ θεοῦ — and calls Abel's offering θυσία, the word this chapter keeps for Cain's.
ἐπεῖδεν
ἐφοράω, to oversee, observe, and of the gods to watch over, take notice of. The Hebrew wayyišaʿ is he looked with regard. Neither language says why.

Middle Liddell gives πρωτότοκος one sense, first-born, so it stands as plain text; στέαρ is stiff fat, tallow, suet.
καὶ αὐτός
καί as also: he too brought.

Notes

Lexical range, aspect, and where the Greek parts from the Hebrew

ἐλύπησεν … περίλυπος
λυπέω, to give pain to, distress, grieve. divergence The Hebrew has wayyiḥar lĕqayin, it burned to Cain — anger — and at 4:6 asks why are you angry? The Greek makes it grief both times: ἐλύπησεν here, περίλυπος, deeply grieved, there.
ἐλύπησεν τὸν Καιν
No subject is named: it grieved Cain.
οὐ προσέσχεν
προσέχω's first sense is to hold to, offer; to turn one's mind to, give heed to follows. God did not turn to Cain's offering.
συνέπεσεν τῷ προσώπῳ
Fell together in the face. συμπίπτω is to fall together — of armies meeting, of things coinciding. The Hebrew is his face fell; at 4:6 the face is the subject.

Notes

Lexical range, aspect, and where the Greek parts from the Hebrew

Ἵνα τί
In order that what? — ἵνα τί γένηται, that what may happen: the Greek idiom for why, which the New Testament prints as one word, ἱνατί. ἵνα takes its conjunction sense, and τί stands as plain text.
περίλυπος
Deeply grieved, Middle Liddell's one sense, so plain text. It is the word of Mark 14:34, Περίλυπός ἐστιν ἡ ψυχή μου ἕως θανάτου.
Ἵνα
Capitalised because it opens direct speech, as Rahlfs prints it; listed in `speech` so the checks do not take it for a proper name.

Notes

Lexical range, aspect, and where the Greek parts from the Hebrew

ἐὰν ὀρθῶς προσενέγκῃς, ὀρθῶς δὲ μὴ διέλῃς, ἥμαρτες; ἡσύχασον
If you brought it rightly but did not divide it rightly, did you not sin? Be still. divergence The Hebrew reads if you do well, is there not a lifting up? and if you do not do well, sin crouches at the door — lappetaḥ ḥaṭṭāʾt rōbēṣ. The Greek has an offering correctly brought and wrongly cut: διαιρέω, to take one from another, divide into parts. Where the Hebrew has sin as a noun lying in wait, the Greek has ἥμαρτες, a verb in a question; where the Hebrew has it crouching, the Greek has ἡσύχασον, be still, said to Cain.
ἥμαρτες
ἁμαρτάνω's first sense is to miss, miss the mark, of a spear; to fail, do wrong, err, sin comes after.
πρὸς σὲ ἡ ἀποστροφὴ αὐτοῦ, καὶ σὺ ἄρξεις αὐτοῦ
The words spoken to the woman at 3:16 — πρὸς τὸν ἄνδρα σου ἡ ἀποστροφή σου, καὶ αὐτός σου κυριεύσει — turned toward Cain. αὐτοῦ is masculine; the Greek sentence has no noun for sin, and the masculine in view is the brother.
ἄρξεις
ἄρχω's first numbered sense is to begin, make a beginning; to lead, rule, govern, with the genitive as here, is its second.
ὀρθῶς
The adverb of ὀρθός, filed inside the adjective's entry: straight, then right, true, correct.

Notes

Lexical range, aspect, and where the Greek parts from the Hebrew

Διέλθωμεν εἰς τὸ πεδίον
Let us go through into the plain. divergence The Hebrew says Cain said to Abel his brother and gives no words; the next clause follows at once. The Greek supplies what he said, as the Samaritan Pentateuch, the Syriac and the Latin also do.
ἐν τῷ εἶναι αὐτούς
The articular infinitive with ἐν: in their being in the plain — while they were.
ἀνέστη … ἐπί
ἀνίστημι's causal senses belong to the present; the aorist ἀνέστη is intransitive, stood up, rose, and with ἐπί, rose against.
πεδίον
A plain, flat, open country, for Hebrew śādeh, the field — the word the Greek rendered ἀγρός at 2:5.
Διέλθωμεν
Capitalised because it opens direct speech, as Rahlfs prints it; listed in `speech` so the checks do not take it for a proper name.

φύλαξ

μή

Ποῦ
Where?, as God asked the man at 3:9.

Notes

Lexical range, aspect, and where the Greek parts from the Hebrew

ἐπικατάρατος σὺ ἀπὸ τῆς γῆς
Yet more accursed, the word of 3:14 and 3:17. At 3:17 the earth was cursed in the man's works; now the man is cursed from the earth. ἀπό is separation, as at 2:2.
ἔχανεν τὸ στόμα αὐτῆς
χάσκω, to yawn, gape: Middle Liddell has no χαίνω and files the aorist ἔχανον here. The earth opens its mouth to take the blood — δέχομαι, to take, accept, receive, a verb that runs on to receive hospitably.

Notes

Lexical range, aspect, and where the Greek parts from the Hebrew

στένων καὶ τρέμων
Moaning and trembling. divergence The Hebrew is nāʿ wānād, a wanderer and a fugitive — words of motion, and nād is the root of the land of Nôd at 4:16. The Greek has words of groaning and shaking, and the play on the land's name is gone.
ἐργᾷ
The contracted future of ἐργάζομαι, you will work — the same form as ἐργάσῃ.
οὐ προσθήσει τὴν ἰσχὺν αὐτῆς δοῦναί σοι
προστίθημι with an infinitive, as at 4:2: it will not add to give you its strength. ἰσχύς is strength, might; Hebrew kōaḥ.

Notes

Lexical range, aspect, and where the Greek parts from the Hebrew

Μείζων ἡ αἰτία μου τοῦ ἀφεθῆναί με
A comparative with a genitive infinitive: my charge is greater than for me to be released. αἰτία is a charge, accusation, then the guilt it implies, then a cause; ἀφίημι is to send forth, let go, set free, the verb the New Testament uses for forgiving. The Hebrew gādôl ʿăwōnî minnĕśōʾ is as double: ʿāwōn is guilt or its punishment, and nāśāʾ is to bear or to forgive.
Μείζων
μέγας's first sense is big, so its comparative μείζων is bigger.
Μείζων
Capitalised because it opens direct speech, as Rahlfs prints it; listed in `speech` so the checks do not take it for a proper name.

Notes

Lexical range, aspect, and where the Greek parts from the Hebrew

Οὐχ οὕτως
Not so. divergence The Hebrew is lākēn, therefore. lōʾ kēn, not so, differs from it by one letter, and the Greek renders that.
ἑπτὰ ἐκδικούμενα παραλύσει
For the Hebrew šibʿātayim yuqqām, he will be avenged sevenfold. ἐκδικέω is to avenge, punish; παραλύω is to loose from the side, detach, undo. The words are plain and the sense is not: every one who killed Cain will loose seven things being avenged.
τοῦ μὴ ἀνελεῖν αὐτόν
ἀναιρέω's first sense is to take up, raise; to make away with, destroy, kill is its third. The genitive infinitive gives the purpose: so that no one finding him should take him up.
σημεῖον
A sign, a mark, token; Hebrew ʾôt. Neither says what it was.
Οὐχ
Capitalised because it opens direct speech, as Rahlfs prints it; listed in `speech` so the checks do not take it for a proper name.

Notes

Lexical range, aspect, and where the Greek parts from the Hebrew

Ναιδ
name Hebrew Nôd, wandering — the root of the nād of 4:12, which the Greek rendered τρέμων. Transliterated, it names a land and no longer says what Cain is.
κατέναντι Εδεμ
name Over against Eden; Hebrew qidmat-ʿēden, east of Eden. Εδεμ is glossed again, first in this chapter.
ᾤκησεν
οἰκέω, to inhabit, occupy; to dwell, live, be settled is its second sense.

ἦν οἰκοδομῶν πόλιν
Imperfect with a participle, was building: the work under way, not finished. οἰκοδομέω, to build a house, the verb of the rib at 2:22.
ἐπωνόμασεν … ἐπὶ τῷ ὀνόματι
ἐπονομάζω, to give a surname, to name, with ἐπί and ὄνομα: the city is named upon the son's name.
Ενωχ
name Hebrew Ḥănôk, usually connected with ḥānak, to dedicate. Seth's descendant at 5:18 has the same name, and the Greek spells both alike.

Notes

Lexical range, aspect, and where the Greek parts from the Hebrew

Μαθουσαλα
divergence The Hebrew names this man Mĕtûšāʾēl, and Seth's descendant at 5:21 Mĕtûšelaḥ — two names. The Greek gives both the one name, Μαθουσαλα; with Ενωχ and Λαμεχ in both lines as well, Cain's line and Seth's read more alike in Greek than in Hebrew.
ἐγενήθη
Aorist passive of γίνομαι, came into being, where the Hebrew has wayyiwwālēd, was born. The same entry as ἐγένετο.
Γαιδαδ, Μαιηλ, Λαμεχ
name Hebrew ʿÎrād, Mĕḥûyāʾēl and Lemek. In Γαιδαδ, Γ renders the Hebrew ʿayin, as in Γομορρα, and δ stands where the Hebrew has r — two letters easily confused.

ὁ πατὴρ οἰκούντων ἐν σκηναῖς κτηνοτρόφων

Ιωβελ
name Hebrew Yābāl. Ιωβελ here and Ιουβαλ in the next verse render two names usually connected with one Hebrew root, yābal, to lead, bring.

Notes

Lexical range, aspect, and where the Greek parts from the Hebrew

Αδα καὶ Σελλα, ἀκούσατέ μου τῆς φωνῆς
Rahlfs sets 4:23–24 as verse — six lines, in pairs — the first lines of the book he prints that way. The Greek here is kept on one line, and the lineation recorded here; Αδα and Σελλα open the song, vocative.
εἰς τραῦμα … εἰς μώλωπα
εἰς of cause or result: a man for a wound to me. μώλωψ has no Middle Liddell entry; LSJ gives mark of a stripe, weal, bruise. It is the word of Isaiah 53:5, and of 1 Peter 2:24, οὗ τῷ μώλωπι ἰάθητε.
ἐνωτίσασθε
ἐνωτίζομαι, from οὖς, ear: to hearken to, one sense, so plain text. It renders Hebrew haʾăzēnnâ, likewise from ʾōzen, ear.
ἄνδρα … νεανίσκον
ἀνήρ, a man, and νεανίσκος, a youth, one sense and plain text; the Hebrew has ʾîš and yeled, a boy.

Notes

Lexical range, aspect, and where the Greek parts from the Hebrew

ἑβδομηκοντάκις ἑπτά
Word for word, seventy times seven. The Hebrew is šibʿîm wĕšibʿâ, seventy-seven, and the Greek can be read either way. Matthew 18:22 has the same pair, where Jesus answers how often to forgive: Οὐ λέγω σοι ἕως ἑπτάκις ἀλλὰ ἕως ἑβδομηκοντάκις ἑπτά. LSJ cites the word from these two verses and nowhere else.
ἐκδεδίκηται
Perfect of ἐκδικέω, to avenge, punish: vengeance taken and standing.
ἑπτάκις, ἑβδομηκοντάκις, ἑπτά
One sense each — seven times, seventy times, seven — so plain text.

Notes

Lexical range, aspect, and where the Greek parts from the Hebrew

Σηθ … Ἐξανέστησεν
divergence The Hebrew names Šēt from šāt, he has appointed: God has appointed me another seed. The Greek has ἐξανίστημι, to raise up, and the name no longer explains itself — as with Καιν at 4:1.
σπέρμα ἕτερον
σπέρμα, that which is sown, the word of 3:15; ἕτερος is the other of two.
λέγουσα
Feminine: the woman names him and speaks, as in the Hebrew.
Σηθ
name Hebrew Šēt.
Ἐξανέστησεν
Capitalised because it opens direct speech, as Rahlfs prints it; listed in `speech` so the checks do not take it for a proper name.

Notes

Lexical range, aspect, and where the Greek parts from the Hebrew

ἤλπισεν ἐπικαλεῖσθαι
This one hoped to call upon the name. divergence The Hebrew is ʾāz hûḥal liqrōʾ bĕšēm YHWH, then it was begun to call on the name of YHWH — a beginning. The Greek has a man who hoped, the sense of yāḥal, and no then.
κυρίου τοῦ θεοῦ
divergence The Hebrew has YHWH alone; the Greek has κύριος for the name, and adds τοῦ θεοῦ.
Ενως
name Hebrew ʾĕnôš, which is also the common noun man, mankind, as ʾādām is.

Notes

Lexical range, aspect, and where the Greek parts from the Hebrew

Αὕτη ἡ βίβλος γενέσεως
The heading of 2:4, word for word as far as γενέσεως. Matthew 1:1 opens the New Testament with the same two nouns: Βίβλος γενέσεως Ἰησοῦ χριστοῦ. βίβλος is first the inner bark of the papyrus; a book is its third sense.
ἀνθρώπων … τὸν Αδαμ
divergence The Hebrew has ʾādām both times: the book of the generations of ʾādām, in the day God created ʾādām. The Greek reads the first as the common noun, in the plural, of men, and the second as the name.
κατʼ εἰκόνα θεοῦ ἐποίησεν αὐτόν
The words of 1:27, where the Greek has τὸν ἄνθρωπον for τὸν Αδαμ. divergence The Hebrew here is bidmût ʾĕlōhîm, in the likeness of God: dĕmût, which 1:26 rendered ὁμοίωσις, is εἰκών here, the word 1:26–27 keep for ṣelem, image.
ἐποίησεν … ἐποίησεν
divergence The Hebrew has bĕrōʾ … ʿāśâ, created … made. The Greek has ποιέω for both, as for bārāʾ at 1:1.
κατʼ εἰκόνα
κατά with the accusative, according to. The entry heads its cases together and opens down, so down is the headword, as at 2:8 and 2:18. εἰκών is a likeness, image, portrait, then an image in a mirror, a phantom, a simile: from ἔοικα, to be like.
ἀνθρώπων
The 1950 printing reads ἀνθρπώπων, with a stray π, a misprint for no word; the transcription corrects it. The 1935 first printing, which is lending-only, could not be checked.
Αδαμ
name Glossed again, first in this chapter.

Notes

Lexical range, aspect, and where the Greek parts from the Hebrew

ἄρσεν καὶ θῆλυ ἐποίησεν αὐτούς
The last words of 1:27, repeated. Jesus quotes them in Matthew 19:4 and Mark 10:6, ἄρσεν καὶ θῆλυ ἐποίησεν αὐτούς, in the answer on divorce. Both adjectives are neuter; αὐτούς is masculine.
ἄρσεν, θῆλυ
ἄρσην is male, then masculine, strong. θῆλυς is female, then, in a second group, fresh, refreshing (of dew), tender, delicate and soft, yielding.
ἐποίησεν … ἐποίησεν
divergence The Hebrew is bĕrāʾām … bĕyôm hibbārĕʾām, he created them … in the day they were created: its second verb is passive. The Greek has the active ἐποίησεν αὐτούς both times.
ἐπωνόμασεν τὸ ὄνομα αὐτῶν Αδαμ
divergence The Hebrew wayyiqrāʾ ʾet-šĕmām ʾādām, called their name ʾādām, uses the common noun, humankind. The Greek transliterates, and the two are given one proper name.
εὐλόγησεν
Without the augment Rahlfs prints at 2:3, ηὐλόγησεν. To speak well of; to bless is the entry's fourth gloss.

Notes

Lexical range, aspect, and where the Greek parts from the Hebrew

διακόσια καὶ τριάκοντα
Two hundred and thirty. divergence The Hebrew has 130, and 800 at 5:4. Down to Enoch the Greek adds a hundred years before each son's birth and takes a hundred from the years after it, except at Jared, where the two texts agree; each lifetime comes out the same. Methuselah and Lamech differ otherwise (5:25, 5:28).
ἔζησεν
Aorist, as every verb of the genealogy's frame is — ἔζησεν, ἐγέννησεν, ἀπέθανεν: each span of years is one completed whole.
κατὰ τὴν ἰδέαν αὐτοῦ καὶ κατὰ τὴν εἰκόνα αὐτοῦ
divergence The Hebrew is bidmûtô kĕṣalmô, in his likeness, according to his image. dĕmût is ἰδέα here, form, the look of a thing: a third Greek word for it, after ὁμοίωσις at 1:26 and εἰκών at 5:1. The Greek repeats κατά and joins the two with καί.
ἐγέννησεν
γεννάω, to beget, engender, of the father. Neither text gives it an object here: begot according to his form.
ἔτη
Middle Liddell gives each numeral one sense, and ἔτος one, a year, so every number and every years in the chapter is plain text.
Σηθ
name Hebrew Šēt; see 4:25.

Notes

Lexical range, aspect, and where the Greek parts from the Hebrew

ἑπτακόσια
divergence The Hebrew has 800.
ἐγένοντο … ἑπτακόσια ἔτη
The days came to be seven hundred years: γίνομαι with the years as its predicate, in the nominative.
μετὰ τὸ γεννῆσαι αὐτόν
μετά with the articular infinitive, after his begetting, with αὐτόν its subject. The accusative's after comes late in the entry, which opens into the middle of, as at 4:3.
υἱοὺς καὶ θυγατέρας
υἱός, a son, and θυγάτηρ, a daughter, have one sense each, so both are plain text.

εὐηρέστησεν
divergence The Hebrew again has walked with God, as at 5:22.
οὐχ ηὑρίσκετο

μετέθηκεν
μετατίθημι, to place among, then to place differently, to transpose, to change. divergence The Hebrew is lāqaḥ, took; the Greek verb is one of changing place.
ὅτι
Hebrews 11:5 quotes the clause with διότι: καὶ οὐχ ηὑρίσκετο διότι μετέθηκεν αὐτὸν ὁ θεός. variant Codex Alexandrinus reads διότι here too, as Rahlfs's apparatus records.

Notes

Lexical range, aspect, and where the Greek parts from the Hebrew

Νωε … διαναπαύσει
divergence The Hebrew explains Nōaḥ with yĕnaḥămēnû, he will comfort us, from nāḥam. The Greek has διαναπαύω, to allow to rest: the sense of nûaḥ, to rest, to which the name is usually connected. In neither language does the verb sound like the name.
διαναπαύσει
Middle Liddell has only the middle, διαναπαύομαι, to rest awhile. LSJ gives the active: to allow to rest awhile, to interrupt, to relieve.
τῶν λυπῶν
λύπη, pain of body, the word of 3:16–17; at 3:17, as here, it renders ʿiṣṣābôn.
καὶ ἀπὸ τῆς γῆς
divergence The Hebrew min-hāʾădāmâ, from the ground, has no and before it, and says where the toil comes from. The Greek adds καί, and the earth becomes a third thing named.
ἧς κατηράσατο
καταράομαι, to call down curses upon; the curse is 3:17, ἐπικατάρατος ἡ γῆ. ἧς takes the case of γῆς.
κύριος ὁ θεός
divergence The Hebrew has YHWH alone; the Greek has κύριος for the name, and adds ὁ θεός.
Νωε
name Hebrew Nōaḥ. Luke 3:36 has Νῶε.
Οὗτος
Capitalised because it opens direct speech, as Rahlfs prints it; listed in `speech` so the checks do not take it for a proper name.

ἑαυτοῖς

Notes

Lexical range, aspect, and where the Greek parts from the Hebrew

Οὐ μὴ καταμείνῃ
οὐ μή with the aorist subjunctive, the strongest denial: shall by no means stay. καταμένω is to stay behind, stay, then to remain fixed, continue. The Hebrew verb, yādôn, is of uncertain sense.
ἐν τοῖς ἀνθρώποις τούτοις
divergence The Hebrew is bāʾādām, in man, singular and without these. The Greek narrows the saying to these men.
διὰ τὸ εἶναι αὐτοὺς σάρκας
Because they are flesh, διά with the articular infinitive. divergence The Hebrew bĕšaggam hûʾ bāśār is in their erring he is flesh, or since he too is flesh; the Greek has neither, and puts σάρξ in the plural, fleshes.
ἑκατὸν εἴκοσι ἔτη
120, as in the Hebrew.
πνεῦμα
Lower case, as at 1:2: the entry's first sense is a blowing, and spirit comes after wind and breath.
Οὐ
Capitalised because it opens direct speech, as Rahlfs prints it; listed in `speech` so the checks do not take it for a proper name.

Notes

Lexical range, aspect, and where the Greek parts from the Hebrew

οἱ γίγαντες … οἱ γίγαντες
divergence The Hebrew has two words: hannĕpilîm, the Nephilim, who were on the earth, and haggibbōrîm, the mighty men of old. The Greek has γίγαντες for both. Middle Liddell's first sense is the Giants, the sons of Gaia — the mythological race — and lower case here, as the Greek has no capital.
ὡς ἂν εἰσεπορεύοντο
ὡς ἄν with the imperfect, whenever: a repeated going in, and the imperfect ἐγεννῶσαν after it is repeated too.
ἐγεννῶσαν ἑαυτοῖς
The imperfect ἐγέννων, with the ending -σαν. divergence The Hebrew wĕyāldû lāhem is and they bore to them: the women bear. In the Greek the sons of God stay the subject — they begot for themselves.
οἱ ἀπʼ αἰῶνος, οἱ ἄνθρωποι οἱ ὀνομαστοί
The Hebrew mēʿôlām ʾanšê haššēm, of old, men of the name. ὀνομαστός is named, then of name, notable, famous.

Notes

Lexical range, aspect, and where the Greek parts from the Hebrew

ἐπληθύνθησαν αἱ κακίαι τῶν ἀνθρώπων
divergence The Hebrew is rabbâ rāʿat hāʾādām, the evil of man was great, singular. The Greek has the badnesses were multiplied, in the plural. κακία is first badness in quality, then cowardice, then moral badness, wickedness.
πᾶς τις διανοεῖται … ἐπιμελῶς ἐπὶ τὰ πονηρά
divergence The Hebrew is wĕkol-yēṣer maḥšĕbōt libbô raq raʿ, every inclination of the thoughts of his heart was only evil. The Greek has each one ponders in his heart carefully upon the evil things: no inclination, no only, and ἐπιμελῶς, carefully, which the Hebrew does not have.
ἐπιμελῶς
The adverb of ἐπιμελής, careful, anxious about, filed inside the adjective's entry, as ὀρθῶς is at 4:7.
πονηρά
πονηρός is toilsome, painful, before it is wicked, as at 2:9.
κύριος ὁ θεός
divergence The Hebrew has YHWH alone.

Notes

Lexical range, aspect, and where the Greek parts from the Hebrew

ἐνεθυμήθη
ἐνθυμέομαι, to lay to heart, consider well, ponder; to take to heart, be hurt is its second sense. divergence The Hebrew is wayyinnāḥem, and he regretted.
καὶ διενοήθη
διανοέομαι, to be minded, intend, then to think over. divergence The Hebrew is wayyitʿaṣṣēb ʾel-libbô, and he was grieved to his heart. The Greek has no grief and no heart.
ὁ θεός
divergence The Hebrew has YHWH; the Greek has ὁ θεός alone.

ὅτι ἐθυμώθην
θυμόω, to make angry, whose middle and passive are to be wroth, angry. divergence The Hebrew is kî niḥamtî, for I regret. The Greek gives anger as the reason where the Hebrew gives regret, as it gave thought for regret at 6:6.
Ἀπαλείψω
ἀπαλείφω, to wipe off, expunge — of a name from a register. The Hebrew ʾemḥeh is I will wipe out.
ἀπὸ ἑρπετῶν
ἑρπετόν is first a walking animal, quadruped, and a creeping thing, reptile second.
ὁ θεός

Ἀπαλείψω
Capitalised because it opens direct speech, as Rahlfs prints it; listed in `speech` so the checks do not take it for a proper name.

δίκαιος, τέλειος
δίκαιος is first observant of custom and social rule, well-ordered, and righteous second; τέλειος is having reached its end, finished, complete before it is perfect. The Hebrew is ṣaddîq tāmîm.
ἐν τῇ γενεᾷ αὐτοῦ

ἦν κατεφθαρμένη
Was, having been destroyed: the perfect participle with ἦν, a state already reached. καταφθείρω is to destroy, spoil utterly.
κατέφθειρεν
The aorist and the imperfect of φθείρω share this form. The aorist answers the Hebrew perfect hišḥît.
πᾶσα σὰρξ τὴν ὁδὸν αὐτοῦ
σάρξ is feminine; αὐτοῦ is not. The pronoun follows the sense, not the noun's gender. The Hebrew darkô agrees with bāśār, which is masculine.
κύριος ὁ θεός
divergence The Hebrew has ʾĕlōhîm, God; the Greek adds κύριος.

Notes

Καιρὸς παντὸς ἀνθρώπου
divergence The Hebrew is qēṣ kol-bāśār, the end of all flesh. The Greek has καιρός for end and ἄνθρωπος for flesh. καιρός is first due measure, proportion, then a vital part, and of time the right point of time, the critical time.
ἥκει
ἥκω is to have come, be present: a present form with the sense of a perfect.
ἀδικίας
divergence ḥāmās, violence, as at 6:11.
Καιρὸς
Capitalised because it opens direct speech, as Rahlfs prints it; listed in `speech` so the checks do not take it for a proper name.

Notes

Lexical range, aspect, and where the Greek parts from the Hebrew

κιβωτόν
κιβωτός, a wooden box, chest, coffer. divergence The Hebrew is tēbâ, used only of this vessel and of the basket Moses is laid in. The Greek word also names the ark of the covenant, the Hebrew's ʾărôn: Hebrews 9:4 has τὴν κιβωτὸν τῆς διαθήκης, and Hebrews 11:7 and 1 Peter 3:20 this one.
ἐκ ξύλων τετραγώνων
divergence The Hebrew is ʿăṣê-gōper, gopher wood, a word found nowhere else. The Greek has squared timbers.
νοσσιάς
Nests of young birds: Middle Liddell files the word under νεοσσιά. The Hebrew qinnîm is also nests, the usual word for a bird's nest; the Greek renders it exactly.
ἀσφαλτώσεις … τῇ ἀσφάλτῳ
The Hebrew wĕkāpartā … bakkōper, you shall cover it with pitch, repeats one root, and the Greek repeats one too. ἀσφαλτόω is not in Middle Liddell; LSJ gives one sense, smear with pitch, citing this verse, so it is plain text.
τετραγώνων
With four equal angles, rectangular, square: an adjective in the genitive takes of, as πονηρός did at 2:9.

Notes

Lexical range, aspect, and where the Greek parts from the Hebrew

πήχεων
πῆχυς is first the fore-arm, and only in its fourth sense the measure, the distance from the point of the elbow to the end of the little finger, a cubit. The Hebrew is ʾammâ.
τριακοσίων … πεντήκοντα … τριάκοντα
300, 50 and 30, as in the Hebrew. The numbers are plain text.
τὸ μῆκος … τὸ πλάτος … τὸ ὕψος
Three verbless clauses: the length of the box of three hundred cubits, and so on, with the measure in the genitive.

Notes

Lexical range, aspect, and where the Greek parts from the Hebrew

ἐπισυνάγων ποιήσεις τὴν κιβωτόν
divergence The Hebrew is ṣōhar taʿăśeh lattēbâ, a ṣōhar you shall make for the ark — a word for a window or a roof, found only here. The Greek has drawing together you will make the box, and no opening.
εἰς πῆχυν συντελέσεις αὐτὴν ἄνωθεν
To a cubit you will finish it from above, as the Hebrew wĕʾel-ʾammâ tĕkallennâ milmaʿlâ.
ἐκ πλαγίων
From the sides, plural; the Hebrew bĕṣiddāh is in its side. πλάγιος as a noun, τὰ πλάγια, is the sides, the flanks.
κατάγαια, διώροφα καὶ τριώροφα
The Hebrew is taḥtiyyim šĕniyyim ûšĕlišîm, lower, second and third decks. κατάγαιος is under the earth, underground, filed under κατάγειος. διώροφος is not in Middle Liddell; LSJ's one sense is with two roofs or stories, citing this verse. τριώροφος is of three stories or floors. One sense each, so both are plain text.

Notes

Lexical range, aspect, and where the Greek parts from the Hebrew

τὸν κατακλυσμὸν ὕδωρ
The Hebrew hammabbûl mayim, the flood, water, set side by side, and the Greek keeps both. κατακλυσμός, a deluge, inundation, is the word of Matthew 24:38–39, Luke 17:27 and 2 Peter 2:5.
πνεῦμα ζωῆς
The Hebrew rûaḥ ḥayyîm. πνεῦμα, lower case, as at 1:2 and 6:3.
τελευτήσει
τελευτάω is first to complete, finish, accomplish; to end life, to die is its second sense, which is the verse's. The Hebrew yigwāʿ is will expire.
ὅσα ἐάν
ὅσος, as great as, as many as, with ἐάν for ἄν: as many as may be. Perseus's opening Latin, quantus, is left out.

Notes

Lexical range, aspect, and where the Greek parts from the Hebrew

τὴν διαθήκην
Covenant, Hebrew bĕrît. Middle Liddell's first sense is a disposition of property by will, a will, testament; an arrangement between two parties, covenant is its second. Hebrews 9:16 turns on the first: ὅπου γὰρ διαθήκη, θάνατον ἀνάγκη φέρεσθαι τοῦ διαθεμένου.
στήσω
ἵστημι in its causal tenses, to make to stand, set. The Hebrew wahăqimōtî is also I will cause to stand.
πρὸς σέ
πρός with the accusative, toward you; the Hebrew ʾittāk is with you.
μετὰ σοῦ
μετά with the genitive, the pronoun as plain text, as at 3:6.

Notes

Lexical range, aspect, and where the Greek parts from the Hebrew

δύο δύο
Two two, a distributive, two by two. divergence The Hebrew here is šnayim mikkōl, two of every; the doubled form is the Hebrew's at 7:9.
ἵνα τρέφῃς μετὰ σεαυτοῦ
divergence The Hebrew is lĕhaḥăyōt ʾittāk, to keep alive with you. The Greek has τρέφω, whose first sense in Middle Liddell is to thicken or congeal a liquid, to curdle milk; to make to grow, bring up, rear is its second, and to maintain, support comes later. The headword keeps the lexicon's order.
ἀπὸ πάντων τῶν κτηνῶν καὶ … τῶν ἑρπετῶν καὶ … τῶν θηρίων
The Hebrew has from all the living, from all flesh; the Greek names cattle, creeping things and wild animals before all flesh.
ἄρσεν καὶ θῆλυ
The words of 1:27 and 5:2, now of the animals.

Notes

Lexical range, aspect, and where the Greek parts from the Hebrew

κατὰ γένος
According to kind, the Hebrew lĕmînô. γένος is first race, stock, family, and a class, sort, kind late in the entry.
τρέφεσθαι
The present infinitive, middle or passive: the first sense, to thicken, in that voice. The entry's passive glosses, to become firm and to be reared, grow up, follow in the chain.
ἄρσεν καὶ θῆλυ
divergence Not in the Hebrew of this verse, which ends to keep alive.
τῶν ὀρνέων τῶν πετεινῶν
Two words for birds: ὄρνεον, a bird, and πετεινόν, winged fowl. The Hebrew has hāʿôp alone, and the Greek adds πάντων before it.

τῶν καθαρῶν
καθαρός is first clear of dirt, clean, spotless, then clear, open, and in a moral sense clear from pollution, pure. The Hebrew is haṭṭĕhôrâ.
ἑπτὰ ἑπτά, ἄρσεν καὶ θῆλυ
divergence The Hebrew is šibʿâ šibʿâ ʾîš wĕʾištô, seven seven, a man and his wife, and of the unclean šnayim ʾîš wĕʾištô. The Greek has male and female, the words of 1:27.
εἰσάγαγε
εἰσάγω, to lead in, the verb of 6:19, now an aorist imperative.

καὶ ἀπὸ τῶν πετεινῶν τῶν μὴ καθαρῶν δύο δύο
divergence Not in the Hebrew, which has only of the birds of the heavens, seven seven, male and female. The Greek adds clean to those birds and a second clause for the unclean, matching 7:2.
διαθρέψαι σπέρμα
The Hebrew is lĕḥayyôt zeraʿ, to keep seed alive. διατρέφω has one sense in Middle Liddell, to sustain continually, so it is plain text.
ἐπὶ πᾶσαν τὴν γῆν
divergence The Hebrew is ʿal-pĕnê kol-hāʾāreṣ, upon the face of all the earth. The Greek has no face.

Notes

Lexical range, aspect, and where the Greek parts from the Hebrew

πᾶσαν τὴν ἐξανάστασιν
divergence The Hebrew is kol-hayqûm, all that stands, every living substance, from qûm, to rise, stand. The Greek renders the root: ἐξανάστασις, a rising up from, which Middle Liddell glosses resurrection and knows only from Philippians 3:11, εἰς τὴν ἐξανάστασιν τὴν ἐκ νεκρῶν. At 7:23 the same Hebrew word is ἀνάστημα. Codex Alexandrinus reads πᾶν τὸ ἀνάστημα here too, as Rahlfs's apparatus records.
ἐξαλείψω
ἐξαλείφω's first sense is to plaster or wash over, used of walls; to wipe out, obliterate is its second. The Hebrew ʾemḥeh is I will wipe out, as at 6:7, where the Greek had ἀπαλείφω.
ἐπάγω ὑετόν
divergence The Hebrew is ʾānōkî mamṭîr, I am causing it to rain. The Greek has I bring rain, with ἐπάγω, the verb of the deluge at 6:17.
τεσσαράκοντα νύκτας
νύξ is, in Middle Liddell's words, night, either the night-season or a night; the first tagged translation is the night-season.

The deluge of water came to be. The Hebrew wĕhammabbûl hāyâ mayim sets the flood and waters side by side. variant Rahlfs prints ἐγένετο ὕδατος from Papyrus 911 alone; Codex Alexandrinus alone has ἦν.
ἐτῶν ἑξακοσίων
Genitive of age, as at 5:32; the Hebrew is a son of six hundred years.
