Notes

Lexical range, aspect, and where the Greek parts from the Hebrew

ἀπὸ τῶν πετεινῶν
divergence The Hebrew runs from the clean animal, and from the animal that is not clean, and from the bird, and from everything that creeps on the ground. The Greek puts the birds first.
τῶν μὴ καθαρῶν
variant Codex Alexandrinus adds καὶ ἀπὸ τῶν πετεινῶν after it, marked in the Hexaplaric manuscripts with an asterisk; Rahlfs follows Papyrus 911 in leaving it out.
τῶν ἐπὶ τῆς γῆς
No verb: the sentence runs on into 7:9, where δύο δύο εἰσῆλθον completes it. Rahlfs prints no stop.

On the seventh and twentieth of the month. divergence The Hebrew is bĕšibʿâ-ʿāśār yôm laḥōdeš, on the seventeenth day of the month. εἰκάς is the twentieth day of the month, one sense, and ἑξακοσιοστός, six hundredth, is LSJ's, citing this verse; both are plain text.
αἱ πηγαὶ τῆς ἀβύσσου
divergence The Hebrew is maʿyĕnôt tĕhôm rabbâ, the springs of the great deep; the Greek has no great. ἄβυσσος is the word of 1:2.
οἱ καταρράκται τοῦ οὐρανοῦ
divergence The Hebrew is ʾărubbōt haššāmayim, the windows of the heavens, in the plural. καταρράκτης as a noun is broken water, a waterfall, then a portcullis, then a gull, the bird that rushes down.
ἐρράγησαν, ἠνεῴχθησαν
Both passive: ῥήγνυμι, to break, and ἀνοίγνυμι, to open, in that voice. The entry's own passive glosses, to burst and to stand open, follow in the chains.

Notes

Lexical range, aspect, and where the Greek parts from the Hebrew

ἐπεφέρετο ἡ κιβωτὸς ἐπάνω τοῦ ὕδατος
The words of 1:2, where πνεῦμα θεοῦ ἐπεφέρετο ἐπάνω τοῦ ὕδατος: the same verb, the same preposition, the same singular water. not in this text The Hebrew here is wattēlek hattēbâ ʿal-pĕnê hammāyim, the ark went upon the face of the waters. The Greek drops face, as it did at 1:2, and face of the waters must not appear.
ἐπεκράτει … ἐπληθύνετο … ἐπεφέρετο
Three imperfects, where the Hebrew has narrative past tenses. ἐπικρατέω is to rule over, then to prevail; the Hebrew wayyigbĕrû is prevailed.

σφόδρα σφοδρῶς
The Hebrew is mĕʾōd mĕʾōd, very very. σφόδρα is very, exceedingly, violently; σφοδρῶς is the adverb of σφοδρός, vehement, violent.
ἐπεκάλυψεν πάντα τὰ ὄρη … ὑποκάτω τοῦ οὐρανοῦ
divergence The Hebrew is passive, all the high mountains were covered, and has under all the heavens. The Greek makes the water the subject, and has under the heaven.
ἃ ἦν
A neuter plural with a singular verb, as at 7:16.

Notes

Lexical range, aspect, and where the Greek parts from the Hebrew

ἀπέθανεν
The Hebrew is wayyigwaʿ, expired, the verb the Greek rendered τελευτήσει at 6:17.
κινουμένη … κινούμενον
The Hebrew has two verbs, hārōmēś, creeping, and haššereṣ haššōrēṣ, the swarm that swarms. The Greek has κινέω for both.

Notes

Lexical range, aspect, and where the Greek parts from the Hebrew

ὅσα ἔχει πνοὴν ζωῆς
divergence The Hebrew is kōl ʾăšer nišmat-rûaḥ ḥayyîm bĕʾappāyw, all in whose nostrils was the breath of the spirit of life. The Greek has πνοὴν ζωῆς, the words of 2:7, with no spirit and no nostrils.
τῆς ξηρᾶς
ξηρός is dry; as a noun, ἡ ξηρά, dry land, its one noun sense, so it is plain text. The Hebrew is beḥārābâ.

Lexical range, aspect, and where the Greek parts from the Hebrew

ἐμνήσθη
μιμνήσκω is in the active to remind; its middle and passive, the form here and the verb as the New Testament uses it, to remind oneself of, call to mind, remember. The active glosses are left out, as for other verbs filed under their middle.
πάντων τῶν θηρίων … τῶν ἑρπετῶν
divergence The Hebrew has every living thing and all the cattle that were with him in the ark. The Greek lists four kinds, adding the birds and the creeping things.
πνεῦμα
The word of 1:2, πνεῦμα θεοῦ, and the Hebrew is the word of 1:2 too, rûaḥ. Middle Liddell's first sense is a blowing; lower case, as there.
ἐκόπασεν
κοπάζω is to grow weary, and of the wind to abate. The Hebrew wayyāšōkkû is subsided.
Νωε
name Glossed again, first in this chapter.

ἐνεδίδου τὸ ὕδωρ πορευόμενον … ἐνεδίδου
The Hebrew wayyāšubû hammayim … hālôk wāšôb, the waters returned … going and returning. The Greek keeps the doubling with a participle and the verb repeated: ἐνδίδωμι, to give in, give way, in the imperfect.
ἠλαττονοῦτο
ἐλαττονόω is not in Middle Liddell; LSJ's one sense is diminish, citing this verse for the passive, so it is plain text.

Notes

Lexical range, aspect, and where the Greek parts from the Hebrew

ἑβδόμῃ καὶ εἰκάδι
divergence The Hebrew is bĕšibʿâ-ʿāśār yôm, on the seventeenth day, as at 7:11, where the Greek also had the twenty-seventh.
ἐκάθισεν
καθίζω is first causal, to make to sit down, seat; to sit down is its later, intransitive use, which the verse has. The headword keeps the lexicon's order, as ὑπνόω did at 2:21.
τὰ ὄρη τὰ Αραρατ
The mountains, those of Ararat: the second article turns the name into a genitive modifier, the Hebrew hārê ʾărārāṭ.
Αραρατ
name Hebrew ʾĂrārāṭ.

καὶ ἐξελθὼν οὐχ ὑπέστρεψεν
divergence The Hebrew is wayyēṣēʾ yāṣôʾ wāšôb, it went out, going out and returning, until the waters dried. The Greek has did not return, and adds to see whether the water had grown weary.
τὸν κόρακα
κόραξ, a raven or carrion-crow; the first tagged translation is carrion-crow.
κεκόπακεν
Perfect of κοπάζω, to grow weary: the water standing abated.

Notes

Lexical range, aspect, and where the Greek parts from the Hebrew

ἀνάπαυσιν τοῖς ποσὶν αὐτῆς
The Hebrew is mānôaḥ lĕkap-raglāh, a resting place for the sole of her foot: mānôaḥ is from nûaḥ, the root of Noah's name. ἀνάπαυσις, repose, rest, is from ἀναπαύω, as διαναπαύσει at 5:29 was.
ἐπὶ παντὶ προσώπῳ πάσης τῆς γῆς
The Hebrew ʿal-pĕnê kol-hāʾāreṣ has face, and so does the Greek, which adds παντί.
ὑπέστρεψεν
variant Codex Alexandrinus reads ἀνέστρεψεν.

ἐπισχών
ἐπέχω is first to have or hold upon; to stay, stop, wait, pause is its fourth sense, which the verse means. The Hebrew wayyāḥel is he waited.
πάλιν

Notes

Lexical range, aspect, and where the Greek parts from the Hebrew

φύλλον ἐλαίας κάρφος
divergence The Hebrew is wĕhinnēh ʿălēh-zayit ṭārāp bĕpîhā, and behold, a freshly plucked olive leaf in her mouth. The Greek has no behold, and for freshly plucked has κάρφος, a dry stalk, dry twigs, such as birds build nests of.
ἀνέστρεψεν
ἀναστρέφω is first to turn upside down, upset; to turn back, return is its second sense.
τὸ πρὸς ἑσπέραν
Toward evening, the article with a prepositional phrase; the Hebrew lĕʿēt ʿereb.

Notes

Lexical range, aspect, and where the Greek parts from the Hebrew

ἐν τῇ ζωῇ τοῦ Νωε
divergence Not in the Hebrew of this verse, which has in the six hundred and first year, in the first month, on the first of the month. The Greek repeats the phrase of 7:11.
ἐξέλιπεν τὸ ὕδωρ
divergence The Hebrew is ḥārĕbû hammayim, the waters dried. ἐκλείπω is first to leave out, omit, then to forsake, and intransitively to fail, cease.
ἀπεκάλυψεν … τὴν στέγην
The Hebrew is wayyāsar … ʾet-miksēh hattēbâ, removed the covering of the ark. ἀποκαλύπτω, to uncover, the verb of revelation in the New Testament; στέγη, a roof.
εἶδεν ὅτι ἐξέλιπεν τὸ ὕδωρ ἀπὸ προσώπου τῆς γῆς
divergence The Hebrew is wĕhinnēh ḥārĕbû pĕnê hāʾădāmâ, and behold, the face of the ground was dry. The Greek has that the water had left off from the face of the earth.

Notes

Lexical range, aspect, and where the Greek parts from the Hebrew

αὐξάνεσθε καὶ πληθύνεσθε
The words of the blessing at 1:22 and 1:28. divergence The Hebrew here is third person, that they may swarm on the earth and be fruitful and multiply; the Greek has the second person and no swarm.
πάντα τὰ θηρία … καὶ πᾶσα σάρξ … καὶ πᾶν ἑρπετόν
Nominative, continuing the list of those told to go out at 8:16; ἐξάγαγε then takes them up.
αὐξάνεσθε, πληθύνεσθε
Both the first sense in the passive: αὐξάνω, to make large, increase, and πληθύνω, to make full, increase, multiply. The entry's passive glosses, to grow and to prevail, are in the chains.
σεαυτοῦ
variant Codex Alexandrinus reads σου.

Lexical range, aspect, and where the Greek parts from the Hebrew

θυσιαστήριον τῷ θεῷ
divergence The Hebrew is mizbēaḥ laYHWH, an altar to YHWH; the Greek has τῷ θεῷ. θυσιαστήριον, an altar, one sense, is plain text: the place of θυσία, the offering of 4:3.
ὁλοκαρπώσεις
The Hebrew is ʿōlōt, burnt-offerings. ὁλοκάρπωσις is in neither Middle Liddell nor LSJ; LSJ has the verb ὁλοκαρπόομαι, to be offered as a whole burnt-offering. It stands as plain text, whole burnt-offerings. variant Codex Alexandrinus reads the singular.
ἀνήνεγκεν
ἀναφέρω is first to bring or carry up; to offer comes later in the entry.

Notes

Lexical range, aspect, and where the Greek parts from the Hebrew

ὀσμὴν εὐωδίας
The phrase of Ephesians 5:2, παρέδωκεν ἑαυτὸν … θυσίαν τῷ θεῷ εἰς ὀσμὴν εὐωδίας, and Philippians 4:18. divergence The Hebrew is rêaḥ hannîḥōaḥ, the soothing smell, from nûaḥ, the root of Noah's name; εὐωδία, a sweet smell, one sense, loses the root.
εἶπεν κύριος ὁ θεὸς διανοηθείς
divergence The Hebrew is wayyōʾmer YHWH ʾel-libbô, YHWH said to his heart. The Greek has having been minded, διανοέομαι, the verb of 6:6, and adds ὁ θεός.
διὰ τὰ ἔργα τῶν ἀνθρώπων
divergence The Hebrew is baʿăbûr hāʾādām, because of man. The Greek adds the works and makes the men plural.
ἔγκειται ἡ διάνοια τοῦ ἀνθρώπου ἐπιμελῶς ἐπὶ τὰ πονηρά
divergence The Hebrew is yēṣer lēb hāʾādām raʿ, the inclination of man's heart is evil. The Greek repeats its words of 6:5, ἐπιμελῶς ἐπὶ τὰ πονηρά, with διάνοια, thought, and ἔγκειμαι, to lie in, be involved in.
καθώς
Middle Liddell gives καθώς first as = καθά, according as, then how.
Οὐ
Capitalised because it opens direct speech, as Rahlfs prints it; listed in `speech` so the checks do not take it for a proper name.

Notes

Lexical range, aspect, and where the Greek parts from the Hebrew

θέρος καὶ ἔαρ
divergence The Hebrew is qayiṣ wāḥōrep, summer and winter. The Greek has ἔαρ, spring.
οὐ καταπαύσουσιν
The Hebrew lōʾ yišbōtû, shall not cease, from šābat. The Greek has καταπαύω, the verb of 2:2–3, where God rested on the seventh day, and the Hebrew there is šābat too.
πάσας τὰς ἡμέρας τῆς γῆς
The Hebrew has ʿōd, yet, while: while all the days of the earth remain. The Greek has the days alone, in the accusative of time.

αὐξάνεσθε καὶ πληθύνεσθε

κατακυριεύσατε
κατακυριεύω has one sense in Middle Liddell, to gain dominion over, so it is plain text.

Notes

Lexical range, aspect, and where the Greek parts from the Hebrew

ὁ τρόμος … ὁ φόβος
The Hebrew is môraʾăkem wĕḥittĕkem, the fear of you and the dread of you. τρόμος is a trembling, quaking; φόβος is first flight, its only sense in Homer, and fear after it.
ὑπὸ χεῖρας ὑμῖν δέδωκα
divergence The Hebrew is bĕyedkem nittānû, into your hand they are given, passive. The Greek has God speak, under hands to you I have given, in the perfect: a gift that stands.
ὑπὸ χεῖρας
ὑπό with the accusative: Middle Liddell's first sense for that case is towards and under, motion that ends beneath. The phrase is the idiom into your power.
ἐπὶ πάντας τοὺς ἰχθύας
variant Codex Alexandrinus leaves out the last ἐπί.

Lexical range, aspect, and where the Greek parts from the Hebrew

ἐκ χειρὸς ἀνθρώπου ἀδελφοῦ
divergence The Hebrew has two phrases, miyyad hāʾādām miyyad ʾîš ʾāḥîw, from the hand of man, from the hand of each man's brother. The Greek has one, from hand of man, of brother.
ἐκζητήσω
ἐκζητέω, to seek out, and to demand an account of. Luke 11:50–51 joins it to the verb of 9:6: ἵνα ἐκζητηθῇ τὸ αἷμα πάντων τῶν προφητῶν τὸ ἐκκεχυμένον … ἀπὸ αἵματος Ἅβελ.
τὸ ὑμέτερον αἷμα τῶν ψυχῶν ὑμῶν
Your blood, that of your lives: the possessive adjective and the pronoun both, as the Hebrew dimkem lĕnapšōtêkem.

ἀντὶ τοῦ αἵματος αὐτοῦ ἐκχυθήσεται
divergence The Hebrew is šōpēk dam hāʾādām bāʾādām dāmô yiššāpēk, whoever sheds the blood of man, by man shall his blood be shed. The Greek has no by man: the one pouring out blood of a man, over against his blood, will be poured out.
ἐποίησα
divergence I made: the Hebrew is ʿāśâ, he made, of God in the third person.
ἐν εἰκόνι θεοῦ
The Hebrew bĕṣelem ʾĕlōhîm, the phrase of 1:27, where the Greek had κατʼ εἰκόνα θεοῦ.
ἐκχυθήσεται
ἐκχέω, to pour out, in the future passive; the entry's own senses for the passive, from to stream out to to lie languidly, stand last.
ἀντί
Middle Liddell gives ἀντί first as over against, opposite, then instead of, at the price of, for. Perseus's summary and the senses for compounds are left out.

Notes

Lexical range, aspect, and where the Greek parts from the Hebrew

ἀνίστημι
I make to stand up: Middle Liddell gives ἀνίστημι its causal senses in the present, and its intransitive ones, to stand up, in the second aorist ἀνέστη of 4:8. The Hebrew mēqîm is the causative of qûm, to stand, and the Greek matches it stem for stem.
τὴν διαθήκην μου
The word of 6:18. Middle Liddell's first sense is a disposition of property by will; covenant is its last.

ἐν τῷ συννεφεῖν με νεφέλας
In my collecting clouds: συννεφέω, to collect clouds, with its cognate object, as the Hebrew bĕʿanănî ʿānān. ἐν joins the articular infinitive as it joins any object, and the infinitive's subject, με, follows as of me, as αὐτούς did at 4:8.
ὀφθήσεται
The future passive of ὁράω, to see: will be seen, the verb of 8:5.

μνησθήσομαι τῆς διαθήκης μου
μιμνήσκομαι, the verb of 8:1, with the covenant: the phrase of Luke 1:72, μνησθῆναι διαθήκης ἁγίας αὐτοῦ.
ὥστε ἐξαλεῖψαι
The Hebrew is lĕšaḥēt, to destroy, as at 9:11, where the Greek had καταφθεῖραι. Here it has ἐξαλείφω, to plaster, then to wipe out: the verb of 7:4 and 7:23.
ὥστε
Used as a conjunction with the infinitive, so the first conjunction sense, so as to; as, as being is the adverb's.

Notes

Lexical range, aspect, and where the Greek parts from the Hebrew

ἧς διεθέμην
divergence The Hebrew is ʾăšer hăqimōtî, which I have established, the verb of 9:9 and 9:11. The Greek has διατίθεμαι, the verb διαθήκη is made from: the disposition which I disposed. Acts 3:25 has the same pair, τῆς διαθήκης ἧς διέθετο ὁ θεός.
διεθέμην
Filed under the active διατίθημι. The entry's senses for the middle, B. Mid., open to arrange as one likes, to dispose of; to make a covenant with is the fourth. The actives are left out, as for other verbs filed under their middle. Hebrews 9:16–17 calls a testator ὁ διαθέμενος.
Τοῦτο
Capitalised because it opens direct speech, as Rahlfs prints it; listed in `speech` so the checks do not take it for a proper name.

ἤρξατο Νωε ἄνθρωπος γεωργὸς γῆς

Lexical range, aspect, and where the Greek parts from the Hebrew

ἐν τῷ οἴκῳ αὐτοῦ
divergence The Hebrew is bĕtôk ʾohŏlōh, inside his tent. The Greek has in his house.
ἐμεθύσθη
μεθύσκω is to make drunk, and Middle Liddell files the aorist passive ἐμεθύσθην under it: was made drunk, with the passive's own to get drunk last.
ἐγυμνώθη
γυμνόω, to strip naked, in the passive. The Hebrew wayyitgal is reflexive, he uncovered himself; the entry gives the passive that sense too, and it is in the chain.
τοῦ οἴνου
οἶνος, wine, one sense, is plain text.

Notes

Lexical range, aspect, and where the Greek parts from the Hebrew

ἐπὶ τὰ δύο νῶτα αὐτῶν
divergence The Hebrew is ʿal-šĕkem šĕnêhem, upon the shoulder of the two of them. The Greek has the two backs of them.
ἐπέθεντο
The aorist middle of ἐπιτίθημι. Middle Liddell's B. Mid. opens to put on oneself or for oneself, and the form takes the first sense in its own voice; the actives are left out.
ὀπισθοφανῶς … ὀπισθοφανές
Neither is in Middle Liddell. LSJ gives the adjective seen from behind, then looking backwards, citing this verse for πρόσωπον, and the adverb one sense, backwards, citing it again; the adverb is plain text. The clause and their face backward has no verb.
συνεκάλυψαν
συγκαλύπτω, to cover or veil completely.
ἐπέθεντο
variant Codex Alexandrinus alone reads ἐπέθηκαν, the active.

παῖς οἰκέτης
divergence The Hebrew is ʿebed ʿăbādîm, a servant of servants. The Greek has two nouns side by side, a child, a house-slave.
παῖς
Middle Liddell's first sense is a child, in relation to descent; a slave, servant is its third, in relation to condition.
Ἐπικατάρατος
Yet more accursed, the one sense of 3:14, plain text.
Ἐπικατάρατος
Capitalised because it opens direct speech, as Rahlfs prints it; listed in `speech` so the checks do not take it for a proper name.

Εὐλογητὸς κύριος ὁ θεὸς τοῦ Σημ
The Hebrew bārûk YHWH ʾĕlōhê šēm. The same words open Zechariah's song in Luke 1:68, Εὐλογητὸς κύριος ὁ θεὸς τοῦ Ἰσραήλ. εὐλογητός has one sense, blessed, and is plain text.
ἔσται
divergence The Hebrew is wîhî, and let … be, a wish. The Greek has the future, will be, and of him for the Hebrew lāmô.
Εὐλογητὸς
Capitalised because it opens direct speech, as Rahlfs prints it; listed in `speech` so the checks do not take it for a proper name.

Notes

Lexical range, aspect, and where the Greek parts from the Hebrew

πλατύναι ὁ θεὸς τῷ Ιαφεθ
The aorist optative, a wish. The Hebrew yapt ʾĕlōhîm lĕyepet plays the verb pātâ, to make wide, against the name Yepet; πλατύνω, to widen, keeps the sense and loses the play.
ἐν τοῖς οἴκοις τοῦ Σημ
divergence The Hebrew is bĕʾohŏlê-šēm, in the tents of Shem. The Greek has houses, as at 9:21.
κατοικησάτω
κατοικέω's first translation, to dwell in as a κάτοικος, leaves its last word in Greek; the headword stops at dwell in.

ἦν

ἐξῆλθεν Ασσουρ
The Hebrew yāṣāʾ ʾaššûr can be read Asshur went out or he went out to Assyria. The Greek has no preposition, and Ασσουρ stands as the subject.
τὴν Ροωβωθ πόλιν
The Hebrew Rĕḥōbōt ʿîr joins ʿîr, city, to the name; the Greek translates it.

Notes

Lexical range, aspect, and where the Greek parts from the Hebrew

ἀδελφῷ Ιαφεθ τοῦ μείζονος
The Hebrew ʾăḥî yepet haggādôl can be read the elder brother of Japheth or the brother of Japheth the elder. The Greek genitive τοῦ μείζονος goes with Ιαφεθ: brother of Japheth the greater.
ἐγενήθη
No subject is expressed: there came to be to Shem also, as the Hebrew yullad gam-hûʾ.

Φαλεκ … διεμερίσθη
The Hebrew plays the name Peleg against niplĕgâ, was divided. The Greek keeps the name and translates the verb, διαμερίζω, to distribute, to divide, and the play is gone.

divergence The Hebrew is ûdĕbārîm ʾăḥādîm, and the same words. The Greek has one sound, φωνή, and adds to all.

ἦν
The imperfect in short, was, and kept on being: the full formula's one would stand beside εἷς's headword.

ἄσφαλτος ἦν αὐτοῖς ὁ πηλός
The Hebrew wĕhaḥēmār hāyâ lāhem laḥōmer, and bitumen was to them for mortar. ἄσφαλτος is the word of 6:14, where the box was smeared with it; πηλός is clay.
δεῦτε
Middle Liddell's one sense holds three glosses, hither! come on! come here!, the plural of δεῦρο.

πλίνθος, a brick, one sense, is plain text.
Δεῦτε
Capitalised because it opens direct speech, as Rahlfs prints it; listed in `speech` so the checks do not take it for a proper name.

τὴν γλῶσσαν … τὴν φωνήν

παύω is to make to cease in the active; the middle, the form here, is to take one's rest, cease, leave off. The actives are left out.

Σύγχυσις
divergence The Hebrew is Bābel, which the verse ties to bālal, to confuse. The Greek translates the name, Confusion, from συγχέω, the verb of the same verse: the play kept, and the city's name lost. At 10:10 it was Βαβυλών.
κύριος ὁ θεός
divergence The Hebrew has YHWH alone the second time; the Greek adds ὁ θεός.
τὰ χείλη
The plural, the lips, where the Hebrew has the singular śĕpat.
αὐτῆς
variant Codex Alexandrinus reads αὐτοῦ, masculine; αὐτῆς, feminine, the city's, is Coislinianus's, M.

ἐν τῇ χώρᾳ τῶν Χαλδαίων
divergence The Hebrew is bĕʾûr kaśdîm, in Ur of the Chaldeans. The Greek has in the land of the Chaldeans, and so does Stephen at Acts 7:4, ἐξελθὼν ἐκ γῆς Χαλδαίων.
ἐνώπιον
Filed inside ἐνώπιος, whose one tagged translation is face to face; the preposition, like Lat. coram, is given no English. One translation, so plain text.
ᾗ ἐγενήθη
The Hebrew môladtô, his birth: in which he came into being.

στεῖρα

Notes

Lexical range, aspect, and where the Greek parts from the Hebrew

Ἔξελθε
The Hebrew lek-lĕkā, go for yourself. The Greek has ἐξέρχομαι, go out of, the verb of Acts 7:3, where Stephen quotes the verse: Ἔξελθε ἐκ τῆς γῆς σου καὶ ἐκ τῆς συγγενείας σου.
τῆς συγγενείας
συγγένεια, first sameness of descent, then kin; the Hebrew môladtĕkā, your birthplace, your kindred.
Αβραμ
name Glossed again, first in this chapter.
Ἔξελθε
Capitalised because it opens direct speech, as Rahlfs prints it; listed in `speech` so the checks do not take it for a proper name.

ἐνευλογηθήσονται ἐν σοὶ πᾶσαι αἱ φυλαὶ τῆς γῆς
Paul quotes it at Galatians 3:8, Ἐνευλογηθήσονται ἐν σοὶ πάντα τὰ ἔθνη, with all the nations from 18:18. Middle Liddell gives ἐνευλογέομαι one sense, to be blessed in one, so it is plain text, and the Greek's own ἐν σοί follows it: will be blessed in in you.
τοὺς καταρωμένους σε
divergence The Hebrew is singular, ûmĕqallelkā, the one who makes light of you, and uses another verb from ʾāʾōr, I will curse. The Greek has the plural and καταράομαι for both.
ἐνευλογηθήσονται
variant Codex Alexandrinus reads εὐλογηθήσονται, without ἐν; the Berlin papyrus, 911, has it.

Notes

Lexical range, aspect, and where the Greek parts from the Hebrew

τὰ ὑπάρχοντα
ὑπάρχω's participle used as a noun, so the entry's first sense for it: existing circumstances, present advantages, then one's possessions. The Hebrew rĕkûšām, their goods.
πᾶσαν ψυχήν, ἣν ἐκτήσαντο
The Hebrew hannepeš ʾăšer-ʿāśû, the souls that they had made: the people acquired in Haran. The Greek has κτάομαι, procured for themselves.
τὴν Σαραν … ἐν Χαρραν
variant Codex Alexandrinus reads Σαρα, and ἐκ Χαρραν; the Berlin papyrus, 911, has Σαραν, and Coislinianus, M, ἐν.
—
Rahlfs prints a dash after the verse, closing a section.

Notes

Τῷ σπέρματί σου δώσω τὴν γῆν ταύτην
Stephen gives the promise at Acts 7:5, δοῦναι αὐτῷ εἰς κατάσχεσιν αὐτὴν καὶ τῷ σπέρματι αὐτοῦ, and Paul reads τῷ σπέρματί σου as singular at Galatians 3:16.
ὤφθη
The aorist passive of ὁράω, was seen: the verb of the appearances in 1 Corinthians 15:5–8.
Τῷ
Capitalised because it opens direct speech, as Rahlfs prints it; listed in `speech` so the checks do not take it for a proper name.

Notes

Lexical range, aspect, and where the Greek parts from the Hebrew

ἡμίονοι
divergence The Hebrew has waʾătōnōt, and she-asses. The Greek has mules, ἡμίονοι, half-asses.
ἐχρήσαντο
χράομαι is first to use; Perseus tags consulting and using an oracle ahead of it, which describe where the sense comes from and are left out. With εὖ, treated well.
μόσχοι
μόσχος has two entries; the second is the animal, a calf, the first a young shoot.

ὁ θεὸς … ἐτασμοῖς μεγάλοις καὶ πονηροῖς
divergence The Hebrew is wayĕnaggaʿ YHWH … nĕgāʿîm gĕdōlîm, YHWH struck … with great strokes. The Greek has ὁ θεός, and adds and toilsome.
ἤτασεν … ἐτασμοῖς
ἐτάζω, to examine, test, with its noun: examined … with trials. ἐτασμός is not in Middle Liddell; LSJ gives it the sense of ἔτασις, trial, affliction.

Notes

Lexical range, aspect, and where the Greek parts from the Hebrew

διαχωρίσθητι
διαχωρίζω, to separate, one sense, plain text, in the passive imperative.
εἰς ἀριστερά … εἰς δεξιά
Neuter plurals used as nouns, so each takes its entry's first noun sense, anarthrous: ἀριστερός left, which is also its first sense; δεξιός right, from the right, where its first sense is on the right hand.
οὐκ … ἐστιν
variant Codex Alexandrinus reads καί for οὐκ, and alone leaves out ἐστιν.

Lexical range, aspect, and where the Greek parts from the Hebrew

τὸν θεὸν … ὡς ὁ παράδεισος τοῦ θεοῦ
divergence The Hebrew has YHWH both times: before YHWH destroyed Sodom and Gomorrah, like the garden of YHWH. The Greek has ὁ θεός both times, and for gan the παράδεισος of 2:8.
— πρὸ τοῦ καταστρέψαι τὸν θεὸν Σοδομα καὶ Γομορρα —
Rahlfs sets the clause between dashes, as the Hebrew sets it apart; the reading keeps it in commas, since dashes mark the chains.
τὴν περίχωρον
περίχωρος is an adjective, round about a place; used as a noun it is the people about in the masculine, the country round about in the feminine, which the verse has.

Notes

Lexical range, aspect, and where the Greek parts from the Hebrew

Ὁ δὲ θεός
divergence The Hebrew is waYHWH; the Greek has ὁ θεός.
πρὸς βορρᾶν καὶ λίβα καὶ ἀνατολὰς καὶ θάλασσαν
The Hebrew ṣāpōnâ wānegbâ wāqēdmâ wāyāmmâ, north, south, east and west. The Greek names the quarters by the north wind, βορρᾶς, filed under Βορέας; the south-west wind, λίψ, one sense and plain text; the sunrise; and the sea.
ἰδέ
The aorist imperative of ὁράω, see.
Ἀναβλέψας … ἰδέ
variant Codex Alexandrinus reads Ἀνάβλεψον … καὶ ἰδέ; the participle is Coislinianus's, M.
Ἀναβλέψας
Capitalised because it opens direct speech, as Rahlfs prints it; listed in `speech` so the checks do not take it for a proper name.

Middle/passive marks a tense in which the two voices share one form; masculine/feminine, an adjective whose form does not distinguish them.

Notes

Lexical range, aspect, and the grammar English cannot reproduce

Ἐν ἀρχῇ
Word for word the opening of LXX Genesis. John is quoting the Greek Old Testament, not the Hebrew. On a Septuagint base the citation is simply visible on the page instead of buried in a footnote — which is the whole argument for reading the Old Testament in Greek alongside the New.
ἦν
Imperfect of εἰμί — and emphatically not ἐγένετο, came to be, which the prologue reserves for created things from verse 3 onward. The entire architecture of the passage rests on this one contrast, and English was carries none of it. Hence the expansion: was already in unbroken existence without any point of having come to be.
ὁ λόγος
Articular. The range: the spoken word, the utterance, the thing said; the account or reckoning, as in rendering an account; ratio and proportion; reasoned discourse; and in Stoic usage the rational principle ordering the cosmos. English Word keeps the speech and drops the reason. Latin had the same problem — verbum won, though sermo held more.
πρὸς τὸν θεόν
πρός with the accusative is directional: toward, facing, up against. It is not παρά (beside), not μετά (in company with), not σύν (together with) — any of which the writer could have used. English with is static; πρός is vectored. This is the largest single loss in the standard versions.
θεὸς ἦν ὁ λόγος
The predicate θεός stands without the article and is thrown to the front; ὁ λόγος carries the article and is the subject. A fronted anarthrous predicate nominative is normally qualitative — it says what the subject is by nature, not which individual it is identical with. So: not the Word was the Father, which the article placement refuses, and not a god, which the fronting refuses. Word order does work here that no English word order can do, which is why this clause has been fought over for eighteen centuries.
Capitals
λόγος and its chain are printed lowercase. The manuscripts have no lower case, so the capital in the familiar Word is not in the text; it is an editorial decision that the noun is a title.
Names
None. λόγος is expanded, not transliterated.

Within, inside of, and by means of the first moment, the origin-point, the source, the first principle from which a thing proceeds, and simultaneously the headship, the rule, and the governing precedence over all that follows, there was, and was continuously, and was already in unbroken existence without any point of having come to be, the utterance, the spoken word, the thing-said, the account, the reckoning, the rationale, the reasoned discourse, the intelligible ordering by which a mind is expressed and by which that mind itself coheres. Notes

Lexical range, aspect, and the grammar English cannot reproduce

οὗτος
Near demonstrative — this one here. It gathers up everything just said and pins it to one referent, which is why the expansion adds and no other.
Function of the verse
It restates 1a and 1b together, and its work is to block a reading in which the θεός of 1c is a different party from the τὸν θεόν of 1b. The one who is God by nature is the same one who stands face to face toward God. The verse looks redundant in English and is not redundant in Greek.
ἦν
The fourth imperfect in two verses. Still no ἐγένετο. The writer is being relentless, and a version that renders all four as a flat was hides the relentlessness.
Names
None in this verse.

Notes

Lexical range, aspect, and the naming rule

Ἐγένετο
Aorist middle of γίνομαι — came to be, came into existence, arose. Placed first for emphasis. This is precisely the verb withheld from the Logos in verses 1–2, and it arrives the moment a creature enters the sentence.
ἀπεσταλμένος
Perfect passive participle of ἀποστέλλω — sent off on another's authority, dispatched with a commission. The perfect makes it a standing status, not a past errand. Root of ἀπόστολος.
Ἰωάννης
name A Greek transliteration of Hebrew Yôḥānān, a compound of the divine name with the verb ḥānan, to show favour or be gracious: Yah has shown favour. The name is kept in the Greek form and glossed in parentheses. It is not translated away, because it is what the man was called; it is not left bare, because to the first hearers it was a sentence.
